Title: Coevolution of Trader Similarity Networks and Follower Dynamics in Social Trading
Authors: Ye Liu, Mingwen Yang, Yong Tan
Abstract: Social trading platforms have been gaining popularity against traditional brokerages over the past few years. Compared with traders on traditional financial markets, those on social trading platforms often exhibit more similar trading strategies. In this paper, we examine the impact of strategy similarity patterns on traders' popularity. We identify two competing effects of similarity: a substitution effect, whereby traders with similar strategies become interchangeable and compete for followers; and a social proof effect, whereby similarity signals credibility in an environment characterized by high uncertainty and limited verifiable credentials, thereby attracting followers. To empirically examine these effects, we construct a dynamic similarity network and develop a coevolution model that captures the joint evolution of network structure and follower dynamics. Using data from a leading social trading platform, we find that, on average, greater similarity leads to a decline in a trader’s followers over time, indicating that the substitution effect dominates. Importantly, this relationship is heterogeneous. For more established traders, the substitution effect is stronger, such that greater similarity reduces their popularity. In contrast, for less established traders, the social proof effect dominates, and similarity increases their popularity. Using counterfactual simulations, we show that reducing the density of the similarity network and promoting a more balanced distribution of followers can mitigate the negative substitution effect, thereby increasing the total number of followers on the platform and, consequently, the platform revenue. Our study identifies several managerial and operational implications for the social trading platforms.

Title: The Role of Ease-of-Return Experience on Contingent Free Shipping Policies
Authors: Ashish Kabra, Wedad J. Elmaghraby, Nitish Jain
Abstract: Contingent free shipping (CFS) policies, whereby consumers get free shipping if their orders exceed a certain amount, are commonplace. Such a policy aims to nudge customers to place larger orders by adding additional items and/or buying more expensive items ( order-swelling ). A less desirable possible outcome is that customers pad their orders to avoid paying the shipping fee but later return the opportunistic or impulse-purchase items ( return-swelling ). A retailer designing the CFS policy’s terms—threshold and shipping fee—should balance these competing effects. We study how the retailer's return environment, specifically the ease-of-return experience (EOR) for customers, moderates order-swelling or return-swelling behavior induced by a CFS policy. We collaborate with an online fashion retailer that switched across multiple CFS policies over time and offered home pickup of returns in some markets but not in others. Our difference-in-differences empirical strategy builds on these policy switches and the location-based variation in the EOR. We find that the EOR can considerably impact the relative profit performance of the CFS policies and that it moderates both the order-swelling and the return-swelling responses. Our counterfactual analysis reveals that return-swelling is the key driver of the observed difference in the relative profit performance of CFS policies across the two EOR market types. Our study documents a novel determinant of the financial performance of a CFS policy: the ease-of-return experience. Our analysis indicates that our collaborating retailer would be better off selecting a (relatively) lenient CFS policy in more convenient EOR markets and a (relatively) stringent CFS policy in less convenient EOR markets.

Title: Revitalizing the Grocery Store Experience: An Empirical Study on the Spillover Effects of Experiential Services
Authors: Bengü Nur Özdemir, Stanley Frederick W. T. Lim
Abstract: Grocery retailers increasingly use experiential services to attract customers to their stores. However, it remains unclear whether these services generate positive spillover effects to core grocery sales or cannibalize existing demand. We provide the first empirical evidence by studying a grocery retailer that introduced a taphouse as its first experiential service and examining the underlying mechanisms. We combine store transaction records with SafeGraph's point-of-interest data and survey data on product attributes. Using a quasi-experimental design, we specify a synthetic difference-in-differences estimator with staggered treatment timings. Our results show significant positive spillover effects. On average, stores that feature a taphouse experienced a 5.97% increase in daily sales volume, a 6.82% rise in sales revenue, a 5.76% increase in transactions, and a 6.18% expansion in product variety compared to stores without a taphouse. Our mechanism analyses suggest that these results are associated with activity through both extensive (newly observed customers) and intensive (greater purchasing activity among existing customers) margins. We find that an average order contains fewer but relatively higher-priced items, leaving average order value statistically unchanged. Newly acquired customers make relatively smaller purchases than existing customers, whose order size does not change significantly following the taphouse introduction. We also find that products complementary to the taphouse and those with a greater propensity for impulse purchasing account for larger shares of grocery sales following taphouse introduction. Finally, nearby competing supermarkets experience reductions in both total visits and unique visitors, suggesting that local competitive substitution may contribute to the observed customer expansion. To assess generalizability, we replicate the analysis with another grocery chain in a different region that introduced a full restaurant and obtain qualitatively similar results. Overall, the findings indicate that adding a taphouse can effectively increase grocery sales volume and revenue. Although high setup costs may deter adoption, our break-even analysis projects recovery in approximately 34 to 39 weeks from grocery-side gross-margin contributions alone, or 27 to 44 weeks when alternative assumptions about taphouse profitability, including operating losses, are incorporated.

Title: Bridging the Gap: The Impact of Online Booking of Healthcare Appointments Service
Authors: Liuyi He, Jifeng Luo, Panpan Wang, Zhiyan Wu, Han Zhang
Abstract: Online healthcare communities (OHCs) play an important role in transforming healthcare delivery. While existing literature has primarily focused on the impact of teleconsultation services on offline demand, the influence of integrating offline access into OHCs on teleconsultation remains largely unexplored. This study addresses the gap by investigating how the integration of offline access into OHCs affects the utilization of teleconsultation services. We leverage a natural experiment in an OHC involving the implementation of the Online Booking of Healthcare Appointments (OBHA) feature, which allows patients to secure in-person visit appointments in the OHC. Using difference-in-differences (DID) models, we find a significant increase in new demand for adopter physicians’ teleconsultation services following the integration of OBHA, without deterioration in service quality. Notably, the increased demand largely comes from patients in remote and underserved areas seeking consultations with high-quality physicians, exhibiting a cascading effect. Furthermore, we find that OBHA adoption extends the geographic reach of physicians’ teleconsultation services and promotes a more equitable distribution of teleconsultation utilization across regions. Our findings indicate that integrating offline access into OHCs not only boosts the utilization of teleconsultation services but also helps reduce health disparities by facilitating access to high-quality resources. This study contributes to the literature on healthcare operations management, healthcare information technology, and health disparities. The insights gleaned from the study also offer practical suggestions to policymakers, OHC operators, physicians, and patients.

Title: Simplifying the Madness of Multiple Entries in March Madness
Authors: Jeff Decary, David Bergman, Carlos Cardonha, Jason Imbrogno, Andrea Lodi
Abstract: Multi-entry betting pools for single-elimination tournaments create a portfolio-design problem: a participant may submit several brackets whose scores are highly dependent, while payouts are typically concentrated on the best-performing entry. Motivated by March Madness pools, we study the problem of selecting a portfolio of brackets that maximizes the expected maximum score (EMS) across entries. This objective captures the top-heavy nature of such contests without requiring a model of opponents' bracket choices, which is difficult to estimate reliably in a tournament played only once per year. We first establish computational and structural properties of the EMS objective. Exact EMS evaluation is #P-hard in general, although it is polynomial-time computable for any fixed number of entries with an exponent that grows with the portfolio size. For two entries, EMS decomposes into single-entry expected-score terms and an expected absolute score-gap term, making explicit the trade-off between selecting individually strong brackets and diversifying across outcomes. These insights motivate two sample average approximation algorithms: an entry-by-entry method based on marginal EMS contributions and a round-by-round method that exploits the geometrically increasing scoring weights in March Madness by emphasizing late-round diversification. Computational experiments using historical tournament data show that the round-by-round method scales reliably and outperforms direct SAA and an entropy-based benchmark for larger portfolios. In a real high-stakes DraftKings pool from the 2023 tournament, our 100-entry portfolio would have achieved a 2.54% probability of attaining a maximum-scoring entry, with higher expected profit than the portfolios submitted by several elite professional bettors.

Title: Impact of Data Privacy Regulations on Recommender Systems Performance
Authors: Liben Chen, Meizi Zhou, Yicheng Song, Gediminas Adomavicius
Affiliations: University of Minnesota, Information and Decision Sciences, Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States; Boston University, Information Systems, Boston, Massachusetts, United States; university of minnesota, carlson school of management, minneapolis, Minnesota, United States
Abstract: Data privacy regulations empower consumers to control the collection of their personal data. A significant consequence of these regulations is their effect on various data-driven business solutions, especially on personalization technologies and recommender systems. We investigate the potential impacts of diverse real-world data privacy practices (that can be adopted by firms in response to various data protection regulations) on the recommender systems performance. We also examine how these impacts vary across different personalization contexts and applications. In particular, we distinguish between scenarios where the user population exhibits more stable vs. more dynamic (i.e., changing) preferences, as these scenarios often represent distinctly different recommendation settings. We use a simulation framework, carefully seeded with real-world data, for a comprehensive evaluation of the recommender system performance under numerous scenarios, such as different recommendation algorithms, different data privacy practices, different degrees of users' preference dynamics, etc. Extensive computational experiments uncover several robust performance patterns for different data privacy practices and highlight substantial differences between recommendation settings with stable vs. changing user preferences. Furthermore, building upon the comprehensive findings from our computational experiments, we propose flexible, parameterizable data privacy practice designs based on the notion of revelation protection. The proposed approach is designed to provide an effective balance between personalization performance and privacy considerations, as demonstrated using extensive simulation experiments. The findings of this study have significant implications for the design of privacy-aware recommender systems in the context of contemporary data protection regulations. The findings can also be informative to policymakers for understanding the practical implications of various data privacy practices and for designing future policies.

Title: A Generative AI-Integrated Framework for Teaching Operations Management: Case-Based Projects
Authors: Sajad Ebrahimi, Raj Bridgelall
Affiliations: Management Department, Seidman College of Business, Grand Valley State University, Allendale, Michigan 49401; Department of Transportation and Supply Chain Management, College of Business, North Dakota State University, Fargo, North Dakota 58108
Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GAI) reshapes business education, instructors must simultaneously safeguard academic integrity and develop students’ AI literacy for an increasingly AI-driven workplace. This study developed the GAI Learning Framework (GLF), a replicable, step-by-step experiential learning approach for case-based projects in undergraduate business courses, illustrated through an operations management (OM) application. Rather than enabling passive cognitive offloading, the GLF promotes active learning by requiring students to craft context-rich prompts grounded in course materials, systematically compare outputs across multiple GAI platforms (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini), and critically evaluate discrepancies against independently verified sources. The framework was implemented across two sections of an undergraduate OM course and evaluated using a student survey that combined Likert-scale items with open-ended reflections (n = 50). All three constructs exceeded the scale midpoint, with pooled means ranging from 3.93 (Constructive Alignment) to 4.08 (Cognitive Load/Scaffolding). Qualitative student reflections further indicated that students perceived the framework as fostering active learning, AI platform literacy, and professional communication skills. This study offers educators a practical, classroom-tested framework for integrating GAI tools into case-based projects in business courses while preserving analytical rigor and promoting experiential learning. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/ited.2026.0224 .

Title: Frontiers: Reducing Disparity Between LLMs and Humans: Optimal LLM Sample Calibration
Authors: Yan Leng, Yunxin Sang, Ashish Agarwal
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to measure human preferences and opinions, but their outputs can diverge from human responses. We introduce human mimicry calibration (HuMCal), a post hoc, model-agnostic method that uses aggregate human benchmark data to learn how to combine LLM outputs from different prompts, personas, and model checkpoints. In applications to consumer transaction data and public opinion surveys, HuMCal improves agreement with human benchmarks over standard aggregation rules, and the calibrated weights often remain useful across time, geography, industry, and question clusters.

Title: Experimental Evidence on Structural State Dependence in Demand
Authors: Sebastian Gabel, Daniel Guhl, Günter J. Hitsch, Kyoung Hwan (Joe) Kook
Affiliations: Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University, Rotterdam 3062 PA, Netherlands; School of Business and Economics, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Berlin, 10178, Germany; Booth School of Business, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois 60637; Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208
Abstract: The paper provides nonparametric estimates of structural state dependence from a natural field experiment for 223 brands.

Title: Injunctive Norms Outperform Reciprocity: Tip Request Messages Can Increase Tipping Without Reducing Demand
Authors: Seung Hyun Kim, On Amir, Kenneth C. Wilbur
Affiliations: Spears School of Business, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma 74078; Rady School of Management, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, California 92093
Abstract: Tip request messages are marketing communications that can help digital platforms balance customer spending with worker effort and compensation. We report the first field experiments testing how three appeals based on tipping motivations—injunctive norms (“It’s customary to leave a tip for the seller’s service”), personalized reciprocity, and impersonal reciprocity—affect tipping and future demand in a global freelance marketplace. Overall, the norms message increased tipping the most, and did so without reducing returning demand, showing that tip request messages can motivate customer tipping to better incentivize and compensate gig workers.

Title: A Learning and Searching Method for Integrated Process Planning and Scheduling
Authors: Hongpei Li, Han Zhang, Ziyan He, Jiaqi Hu, Hongsong Yuan
Abstract: The integrated process planning and scheduling problem combines process route planning and shop scheduling to achieve high efficiency in manufacturing and maximize resource utilization, which is crucial for modern manufacturing systems. Traditional approaches, such as mixed-integer linear programming and heuristic algorithms, often struggle to balance solution quality and computational efficiency, particularly in large-scale scenarios. To address this, we propose learning-then-searching, an efficient framework combining deep reinforcement learning with heuristic search to solve integrated process planning and scheduling problems. We formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and develop a deep reinforcement learning method tailored to capture the complex relationships among operations, machines, and jobs. With the learned policy distributions, Monte Carlo tree search employs learned priors and problem-specific rollouts to further refine scheduling strategies, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation to achieve better solutions. Experimental results show that the proposed framework improves solution efficiency and quality over traditional methods across benchmark and large-scale instances, with pronounced advantages when route ambiguity is high. It also offers practitioners a flexible tradeoff between rapid policy-based decisions and further refinement through tree search when additional computation time is available.

Title: The Problem of Ignoring the Ignorability Assumption in Advertising Measurement: A Matrix Completion Solution
Authors: Omid Rafieian
Affiliations: Cornell Tech, New York, New York 10044; and Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14850
Abstract: This paper frames the overlap violation problem in online advertising auctions as a missing-data problem and proposes a matrix completion approach to correct the resulting bias in observational studies with algorithmic ad allocation.

Title: Contest or Contract: Assessing the Effectiveness of Contests in Online Labor Markets
Authors: Jason Chan, Jiahui Mo, Tingting Nian, Nila Zhang
Affiliations: Carlson School of Management, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota 55455; Poole College of Management, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, North Carolina 27695; The Paul Merage School of Business, University of California, Irvine, California 92697; School of Management, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China
Abstract: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in online labor markets. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: N. Zhang acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72302053]. Title: Multitype Information Acquisition in a Strategic Trading Model
Authors: Hui Ou-Yang, Weili Wu, Xingtan Zhang
Affiliations: Department of Finance, Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, Beijing 100010, China; School of Finance, Central University of Finance and Economics, Beijing 100081, China
Abstract: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72472171 and 72372011]. Title: Inflexibility and Leverage
Authors: Lifeng Gu, Dirk Hackbarth, Yuxin Luo
Affiliations: Sy Syms School of Business, Yeshiva University, New York 10033; Questrom School of Business, Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts 02215; and European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI), 1000 Brussels, Belgium; School of Finance, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China
Abstract: Firms’ inflexibility to adjust their scale persistently explains capital structure variations in a comprehensive sample and randomly selected subsamples. Higher inflexibility leads to lower financial leverage, potentially due to higher default risk and lower value of tax shields. Contraction inflexibility determines leverage more than expansion inflexibility. Moreover, our inflexibility measure explains financial leverage significantly better than other variables that potentially capture certain aspects of adjustment costs for capital or labor. In addition, inflexible firms increase leverage more following a positive credit supply shock. Analyses employing instrumental variables estimation confirm our main finding. Our results suggest inflexibility shapes corporate financial policies. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08672 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance.

Title: Willingness to Compete in Dirty Competitions
Authors: Thomas Buser, Sahar Sangi
Affiliations: University of Amsterdam and Tinbergen Institute, 1018WB Amsterdam, Netherlands
Abstract: Competitive environments often leave room for “dirty” practices such as sabotage, retaliation, or dishonesty. We use an online experiment to document aggregate levels and individual differences in the willingness to engage in dirty competition and in the willingness to enter competitions where the opponent may play dirty. We then use the experimental data to validate a set of survey questions that capture willingness to engage in dirty competition above general willingness to compete. We elicit these questions in a representative survey panel and show that willingness to engage in dirty competition is a strong predictor of holding a management or supervisory position and of working in the private—versus the public—sector, but also of worse self-esteem, worse social relationships, and increased feelings of guilt and shame. Men, younger people, and lower-educated people are on average more willing to engage in dirty competition. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01218 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis.

Title: Robust Auction Design with Support Information
Authors: Jerry Anunrojwong, Santiago R. Balseiro, Omar Besbes
Affiliations: Yale School of Management, New Haven, Connecticut 06511; Graduate School of Business, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027
Abstract: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results hold under other distribution classes that capture “positive dependence,” namely i.i.d., mixture of i.i.d., and exchangeable and affiliated distributions, as well as i.i.d. regular distributions. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02703 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics.

Title: From Employer Responsibility to Environmental Irresponsibility: Unintended Impacts of Social Insurance Law on Pollution Emissions
Authors: Yanan Li, Yu Qin, Wenjun Wang
Affiliations: Business School, Beijing Normal University, Beijing 100875, China; Department of Applied Economics, Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China; Carbon Neutrality and Climate Change Thrust, Society Hub, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou 511453, China
Abstract: This study investigates the unintended effect of the introduction of the 2011 Social Insurance Law on corporate pollution emissions. Using a difference-in-differences framework, our analysis reveals that enhanced social insurance contributions lead to higher industrial pollution emissions, as measured by chemical oxygen demand and wastewater emissions. The mechanism analysis indicates that the enforcement of the law increases firms’ labor costs and financial distress, motivating them to reduce efforts on end-of-pipe treatment activities and measures taken during the production process, which results in higher pollution emission intensity. Our study highlights the potential conflict between employee protection and corporate environmental goals. Further analysis suggests that stronger environmental monitoring and environmental, social, and governance disclosure requirements can partially mitigate this tradeoff, providing valuable insights for policymakers. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Y. Li acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72403026]. Y. Qin acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72342031]. Title: Estimating the Pricing Kernel: A Simple Regression-Based Dimension-Reduction Approach
Authors: Bin Luo, Guofu Zhou, Ti Zhou
Affiliations: College of Business, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen 518055, China; Olin School of Business, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, Missouri 63130; School of Economics and Management, Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen 518055, China
Abstract: We propose a simple framework for estimating the pricing kernel in factor space by constructing the mean–variance efficient factor portfolio via an ordinary least squares formulation with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regularization. The method accommodates high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate factors exceeds the sample size and automatically shrinks redundant factor weights toward zero. We show theoretically that the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the estimated portfolio converges to the theoretical maximum at the fastest rate among existing regression-based approaches. Applying the method to 174 characteristic-based factors together with the market factor, we obtain an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 3.59, substantially outperforming competing strategies and delivering the smallest aggregate pricing errors. The selected factors vary over time in both composition and number, averaging about 50. We further develop a model comparison test and reject the hypothesis that eight widely used sparse factor models are sufficient to span the pricing kernel. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. Title: Tactical Workforce Planning and Deployment with Timing Coordination Requirements
Authors: Gang Li, Anantaram Balakrishnan
Abstract: We address a tactical planning problem facing organizations that must perform geographically dispersed jobs with timing dependencies using appropriate teams of workers and equipment. This Tactical Workforce Planning and Deployment (TWPD) problem, which is motivated by the annual planning and budgeting activity for rail infrastructure maintenance and upgrades, requires making simultaneous decisions on resource sizing and selection, resource-to-job assignment, and resource repositioning to complete all jobs while minimizing resource and transportation costs. Key challenges include timing coordination among jobs, varying resource capabilities, and sequence-dependent changeover costs. Prior scheduling and routing models often focus on short-term decisions, assuming a given set of resources, and do not incorporate complex timing coordination requirements. We propose a large-scale optimization model, with strong timing coordination constraints, that integrates all the features of the TWPD problem. To solve this difficult problem, we propose three new families of valid inequalities to further strengthen the model and develop problem reduction procedures as well as an optimization-based multi-stage algorithm to identify good initial feasible solutions. Our Composite method applies these acceleration strategies before initiating an exact branch-and-bound solution procedure. To test the effectiveness of this method, we first apply it to real data sets for track maintenance from a leading railroad company and compare its performance with a method that uses a standard solver without our enhancements. We find that our method dramatically outperforms the standard method. We also test our method on many randomly generated problems to validate its superior performance and identify problem features that make this problem difficult to solve. When compared to a manual tactical plan, our method quickly generates a near-optimal solution that saves over 15% in annual total cost, demonstrating the practical value and viability of our model and method. We conclude by discussing some managerial implications and insights from our results.

Title: Optimal Return Policies with Heterogeneous Search Rewards
Authors: Fangruo Chen, Weitao Ren, Wenqiang Xiao
Abstract: This paper studies return policy design for an online seller serving consumers who can resolve product-fit uncertainty through costly pre-purchase search, with search rewards varying across consumers. Return policies shape not only post-purchase return behavior but also ex-ante search and purchase decisions, thereby generating endogenous consumer segmentation. One might expect that inexpensive search would reduce the seller's incentive to offer a generous refund. In our baseline model, however, we show that full refund outperforms no refund when search costs are sufficiently low. We trace this result to a fundamental trade-off in implementing a full-refund policy: the search-relief effect versus the return-inducing effect. Full refund substitutes for search by allowing consumers who would otherwise search to purchase directly and evaluate fit after purchase, thereby removing their search-based information advantage and restoring the seller's pricing power. However, it also induces returns from consumers who would otherwise purchase without search and keep the product, sacrificing the revenue generated by their tolerance for misfit. When search costs are sufficiently low, most consumers would otherwise search, and the search-relief effect therefore dominates the return-inducing effect. As search costs fall further, full refund can also achieve a win-win outcome, indicating that pre-purchase search may be socially inefficient. These findings explain when and why sellers may optimally discourage ex-ante search in favor of ex-post product evaluation.

Title: Design and Pricing of Online Dating Subscriptions
Authors: Titing Cui, Michael L. Hamilton
Abstract: Online dating is now the most common way for new couples in the U.S. to meet, with more than 30% of U.S. adults having used a dating app and with global industry revenues exceeding three billion dollars annually. Most dating apps monetize primarily through subscription pricing, offering users fixed periods of access to paid features for recurring fees. However, applying subscription pricing to online dating apps presents some unique challenges. Unlike other digital services, users' valuations of dating app services typically decline with use, as continued participation can be costly in terms of both time and emotional effort, and repeated renewals signal unsuccessful app-mediated searches. Moreover, users who achieve their goal of finding a partner subsequently exit the platform, creating an apparent tension between providing value by successfully matching users and a dating app’s goal of generating profit and sustaining a large userbase of paying subscribers. Given these unique challenges and the transient nature of user engagement with dating apps, it is interesting to note that leading U.S. dating apps, such as Hinge and Bumble, have begun offering increasingly long subscription options, including lifetime subscriptions. In this paper, we analyze the performance of subscription pricing strategies with varying period lengths for online dating platforms. We propose a natural model of dating app monetization and use it to evaluate how subscription length affects both profit and steady-state userbase size. We find that suitably priced lifetime subscriptions can Pareto-dominate all finite-period subscriptions over both objectives, providing a compelling explanation for their emerging use. We then extend our analysis to subscription menus with two options and show that offering one short-term subscription option and one lifetime option guarantees approximately 59.4% of the optimal two-option menu performance.

Title: Machine Learning Instrument Variables for Causal Inference
Authors: Amandeep Singh, Kartik Hosanagar, Amit Gandhi
Affiliations: University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195; The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104
Abstract: A machine learning framework for constructing strong instrumental variables from weak exogenous data achieves semiparametric efficiency with applications to advertising and demand estimation.

Title: Navigating the Rugged Data Landscape: The Impact of Data-Extrapolation Technologies on Knowledge Production
Authors: Soomi Kim
Affiliations: Columbia Business School, New York, New York 10027
Abstract: Data-extrapolation technologies enable progress by importing and applying empirical patterns from one domain to another. Their reliance on empirical patterns, however, is also their limitation: these tools can only be applied where data are abundant. Using the setting of structural biology, I investigate the impact of a data-extrapolation technology on innovation. I exploit the variation in prior data availability to compare areas in which the tool was usable to those in which it was not. I find that the tool increased the quantity of research in data-rich areas: the resulting output yielded limited biological insights but was methodologically rigorous and contributed to downstream research. This paper was accepted by Toby Stuart, entrepreneurship and innovation. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04115 .

Title: Selection into Financial Education and Effects on Portfolio Choice
Authors: Irina Gemmo, Pierre-Carl Michaud, Olivia S. Mitchell
Affiliations: Department of Finance, HEC Montréal, Montréal, Quebec H3T 2A7, Canada; Department of Applied Economics, HEC Montréal, Montréal, Quebec H3T 2A7, Canada; and National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138; National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138; and Business Economics and Public Policy Department, the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104
Abstract: We study the impact of a financial education program on portfolio choices in a setting that allows us to examine both participation decisions and differences in program benefits across individuals. We directly elicit willingness to pay for financial education and show that individuals with higher financial literacy, greater confidence in applying new knowledge, and higher expected returns are willing to pay more. Using incentivized portfolio allocation tasks, we develop outcome measures tailored to individual risk preferences and show that financial education improves decision quality along these dimensions. The program increases the share of participants who experience an improvement by 20 percentage points, corresponding to average gains of 3.2 percentage points of initial wealth. Individuals with the highest willingness to participate benefit disproportionately from the program, with important implications for the design and evaluation of financial education initiatives. By isolating a specific investment skill in a setting with voluntary participation, our design sheds light on how selection into financial education shapes measured program effects and informs the assessment of broader workplace and public training programs. Title: Fulfillment by Platform: Competition and Upstream Market Power
Authors: Amandeep Singh, Jiding Zhang, Senthil Veeraraghavan
Affiliations: Foster School of Business, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195; W. P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona 85281; Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104
Abstract: Fulfillment by Platform: Competition and Upstream Market Power E-commerce platforms increasingly offer fulfillment services that promise faster delivery and easier access to customers. This study shows that these services create a trade-off. Using transaction-level data from a major online marketplace, the authors find that platform fulfillment improves the customer experience and raises consumer welfare, but it also changes competition among sellers. Because fulfillment through the platform adds costs for merchants, smaller sellers with thinner margins must raise prices more than larger sellers. As a result, large merchants gain share while smaller merchants lose ground, increasing upstream market concentration. The findings matter for regulators, platforms, and merchants because they show that a service that benefits consumers can still weaken competition on the seller side. The paper provides rare empirical evidence from both sides of an e-commerce marketplace and highlights why platform policies should be evaluated not only by customer benefits, but also by their effects on market structure.

Title: Corporate Pension Risk-Taking in a Low Interest Rate Environment
Authors: Vasso Ioannidou, Roberto Pinto, Zexi Wang
Affiliations: Bayes Business School, City St George’s, University of London, London EC1Y 8TZ, United Kingdom; and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), London, United Kingdom; Luiss University, Viale Romania 32, Rome, 00197 Italy; and Lancaster University Management School, Lancaster LA1 4YX, United Kingdom; Lancaster University Management School, Lancaster LA1 4YX, United Kingdom; and Dishui Lake Advanced Finance Institute, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai 200433, China
Abstract: We examine how funding deficit pressures shape the risk-taking of U.S. corporate defined-benefit pension plans and how targeted regulatory relief can mitigate these incentives. Using the 2012 Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act reform, which temporarily eased funding pressure by revising discount rate calculations, we show that plans receiving greater relief significantly reduced their equity allocations and shifted toward safer assets. This derisking was most pronounced among active plans and those sponsored by more financially constrained firms. Our findings demonstrate that targeted regulatory relief can curb risk-taking incentives even without altering underlying economic conditions or financial reporting standards and shed light on the likely (and unlikely) frictions driving such behavior. Title: The Equity Market Implications of the Retail Investment Boom
Authors: Philippe van der Beck, Cameron Cohen, Coralie Jaunin
Affiliations: Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts 02163; Université de Lausanne, 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland; and cSwiss Finance Institute, 8006 Zürich, Switzerland
Abstract: We quantify the equilibrium impact of retail traders on the U.S. equity market within a structural model of asset demand. Estimating investor-specific demand curves, we find that Robinhood traders are fundamentally distinct from all other investors, including other households: their demand is the most elastic and tilts most strongly toward volatile and microcap stocks. Each dollar invested through Robinhood generates more than five dollars in aggregate equity repricing, exceeding hedge funds, other households, and all other investor types. We decompose the cross-sectional variation in stock returns during Robinhood’s growth surge in 2020 into investor-specific components and find that shifts in Robinhood traders’ latent demand drove 11% of small-cap return volatility despite their negligible aggregate wealth share. To explain these demand shifts, we show that Robinhood traders are the only investor group whose latent demand is well explained by attention proxies: their demand exhibits a V-shaped response to past returns and rises sharply with trading volume. Our findings suggest that the growth of retail trading platforms represents a fundamental shift in the composition of equity demand with equilibrium consequences disproportionate to retail investors’ share of aggregate wealth. Title: Hybrid Kidney Allocation: Improving Equity by Fair Integration of Deceased Donor-Initiated Chains in Kidney Exchange
Authors: Roby Cremers, Twan Dollevoet, Joris van de Klundert, Michal Andrzej A. Mankowski
Affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam Erasmus School of Economics, Econometric Institute, Rotterdam, ZH, Netherlands; Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez Escuela de Negocios, Department of Operations and Analytics, Viña del Mar, Valparaiso, Chile; NYU Grossman School of Medicine, Department of Surgery, New York, New York, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: Living donor kidney exchange programs (KEPs) expand access to transplants by enabling exchanges among patient-donor pairs. However, highly sensitized patients are disproportionately hard to match and face long waits. Deceased donor–initiated chains (DDICs) have been proposed to enable more transplants by diverting an occasional deceased donor kidney from the waitlist to start a KEP chain, which ends by returning a kidney to the waitlist. Yet, DDICs have seen virtually no implementation. In the U.S., this is largely due to concerns that the kidneys returned may differ in blood-type distribution from those diverted, disadvantaging waitlist patients of certain blood types. We study how DDICs can be integrated into KEPs while explicitly protecting blood-type-specific waitlist access. Methodology/results: We develop two forward-looking optimization approaches: one that solves a stochastic model using Sample Average Approximation (SAA) and one that solves a static model with forward-looking constraints. Through simulation, we show that forward-looking models are needed to preserve the blood-type distribution of donations to the waitlist. Under both models, even limited use of DDICs significantly increases transplant rates for highly sensitized patients. While the static approach requires only modest extensions to models as currently used in practice, the more complex and time consuming SAA-based approach yields larger equity gains. Managerial implications: DDICs can improve access to life-saving transplants for the most disadvantaged KEP patients without reducing access for any blood type on the waitlist. By explicitly controlling the blood-type distribution of waitlist donations, matching policies can address objections that have hindered DDIC adoption, calling for renewed policy evaluation.

Title: Two-Sided Assortment Optimization: Adaptivity Gaps and Approximation Algorithms
Authors: Omar El Housni, Ulysse Hennebelle, Alfredo Torrico
Affiliations: School of Operations Research and Information Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14850; and Cornell Tech, Cornell University, New York, New York 10044; Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, USC Viterbi School of Engineering, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90089
Abstract: On the Power of Adaptivity in Choice-Based Matching Platforms Online labor, lodging, and carpooling platforms decide not only whom users can choose but also when those options are shown. Simultaneity can crowd attention around a few popular users and leave many good matches unrealized. In the forthcoming Operations Research paper, “Two-Sided Assortment Optimization: Adaptivity Gaps and Approximation Algorithms,” the authors study how much platforms gain by updating assortments after observing earlier choices. They compare four policy classes, ranging from showing all assortments at once to fully adaptive policies that process users one by one. They prove that adaptivity within one side improves performance by at most a factor of [Formula: see text], whereas fully adaptive policies improve on one-sided adaptive policies by at most a factor of two; both bounds are tight. They also develop efficient approximation algorithms, extend their results to constrained settings, and empirically show that their methods perform far better than their worst-case guarantees.

Authors: Claire M. Gillan, Stephen M. Fleming, Marion Rouault, Tricia X. F. Seow
Affiliations: School of Psychology, Trinity College Dublin; Trinity College Institute for Neuroscience, Trinity College Dublin; FutureNeuro Research Ireland Centre, Trinity College Dublin; Department of Experimental Psychology and Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience, University College London; Max Planck University College London Centre for Computational Psychiatry and Ageing Research, University College London; Sorbonne Université, Institut du Cerveau–Paris Brain Institute, Institut National de la Santé et de la Recherche Médicale, CNRS, Hôpital de la Pitié Salpêtrière, 47 boulevard de l’hôpital; Functional Imaging Laboratory, Department of Imaging Neuroscience, University College London

Title: Estimating the threat of AI-agent responding across online survey platforms
Authors: Grace Zhang, Robert Walatka, Stephanie Y. Chen, Alexander K. Moore, Oleg Urminsky, Kianté Fernandez, Andrea Low, Jonathan E. Bogard, Craig R. Fox
Affiliations: Marketing, University of Chicago Booth School of Business; Behavioral Science, University of Chicago Booth School of Business; Marketing, London Business School; Marketing, University of Illinois Chicago College of Business Administration; Department of Psychology, University of California; Behavioral Decision Making Area, Behavioral Decision Making Area, Anderson School of Management, University of California; Organizational Behavior, Olin Business School, Organizational Behavior, Olin Business School, Washington University in St. Louis
Abstract: Recent research and advances in LLMs have led to widespread concern that AI agents could pose as human online survey-takers. However, it remains unclear how prevalent AI agents are on survey research platforms and how to effectively detect AI agents. We validated a series of AI detection tests that effectively separated verified-human participants from both prompted commercial and purpose-built AI agents. Using these tests, we collected surveys on seven online platforms and find wide variation in rates of respondents failing AI tests, ranging from 6 to 41% across platforms (compared to a 2.4% false-positive rate for in-person human participants). We further demonstrate that undetected AI agents can impact the results of online surveys. Our findings suggest that while there is an urgent need for AI detection tests and consistent, systematic monitoring of data quality on online platforms, some platforms currently appear to provide data with a low rate of AI agents.

Title: From Chit-Chat to Conversion: Cost-Efficient Conversational Recommendation via Retrospective Learning and Isolated Reflection
Authors: Jiahui Wang, Hongke Zhao, Likang Wu, Bing Lv, Ning Jia
Abstract: Conversational recommendation systems help digital platforms elicit user preferences through multi-turn interaction, but they often face a practical tension between recommendation accuracy and interaction cost when users provide vague or low-information inputs. This study follows a design science approach to develop a cost-conscious conversational recommendation artifact for such ambiguous service encounters. The artifact is guided by two design principles. First, retrospective outcome-guided supervision uses successful historical conversion trajectories as downstream anchors for improving responses at earlier low-information states. Second, isolated reflection separates recommendation generation from consistency checking, enabling diagnostic regeneration when candidate responses conflict with previously stated user constraints. In implementation, the artifact instantiates these principles through parameter-efficient adaptation of open-source large language models and prompt-isolated role switching over a shared backbone model. We validate the artifact on three conversational recommendation datasets covering movie and e-commerce settings, using outcome efficacy, interaction efficiency, process analysis, ablation analysis, robustness checks, and human evaluation. Here, interaction efficiency refers to user-visible dialogue turns, while computational burden is reported separately through training, memory, and latency measurements. The empirical results show that the artifact improves recommendation effectiveness while maintaining a favorable balance between interaction burden and conversion outcomes under the tested conditions. Process-level analysis further characterizes how recommendation behavior evolves over the course of dialogue. This study contributes transferable design principles for embedding retrospective preference optimization and isolated reflection into conversational recommendation systems, offering operational guidance for platforms seeking to improve personalization under constraints on interaction cost.

Title: Do You Lose When You Sell Loose? Impact of Unpackaged Sales on Profit and Waste
Authors: Ismail Kirci, Dorothee Honhon, Alp Muharremoglu
Abstract: Loose sales — the sale of unpackaged products by unit or weight — are frequently promoted as a way to reduce waste because they allow consumers to purchase exactly the quantity they want, rather than being constrained by the fixed quantities dictated by the pre-packaged format. We study a retailer selling a highly perishable product under two possible formats: fixed-size packages and/or loose. The retailer chooses prices and package size to maximize profit. Consumers perceive loose products as fresher, but they also incur an inconvenience cost arising from the additional time and effort required. For the retailer, loose sales carry a higher unit variable cost due to increased labor requirements. In a homogeneous market, we show that, if consumers place substantially higher value on the loose option and its cost is not significantly greater than that of packaged sale, the retailer can make more profit selling only loose at a high price to consumers who buy the quantity they desire. Otherwise, the retailer is better off selling packages of large size, forcing consumers to buy more than they desire to purchase. Interestingly, consumer waste can actually be greater when the product is sold exclusively in loose format. In a heterogeneous market with two consumer segments which differ in the magnitude of their consumption needs, three possible optimal strategies emerge: selling only loose to both segments, selling only (relatively small) packages to both segments, or selling (relatively large) packages to high-consumption needs consumers and selling loose to the low-consumption needs consumers. Our results also demonstrate that selling loose instead of or alongside packages can often be a win-win strategy, simultaneously boosting retailer profits and reducing consumer waste compared to selling only packages. However, in some cases, introducing loose sales may increase waste. These findings indicate that retailers may derive financial gains from offering products in loose form; however, they should ensure that the associated sustainability benefits are genuine before positioning it as a green strategy. Likewise, policymakers seeking to reduce food waste should carefully consider product- and market-specific conditions rather than promoting loose sales as a universally effective waste-reduction measure.

Title: When Good Practices Go Too Far: Overshooting in Organizational Culture
Authors: Francisco Brahm, Christoph Loch, Joaquin Poblete
Abstract: Business research has examined how useful practices can be made to spread and develop in organizations. However, practices have been observed “overshooting”: either over-diffusing—too many employees adopt them, including some whose usage is unproductive; or becoming over-sophisticated—the practice becomes too elaborate, reducing organizational performance. Independent models of over-diffusion and over-sophistication have been proposed; this paper integrates both aspects in a simple, unified model of overshooting. We offer a cultural evolution model that studies how interaction dynamics among employees are able to diffuse and stabilize an equilibrium of underperforming cultural practices, at the same time over-developing the practice so its sophistication goes beyond productive levels. People adopt practices from others based on information about the practice’s productive value, but also influenced by social dynamics with other employees, such as status. Our model clarifies the circumstances in which over-diffusion and over-sophistication can arise, and how these two elements of overshooting relate to each other. We map our model in detail to two cases---process management practices (e.g., six sigma) and Uber's aggressive culture---and discuss the managerial implications.

Title: Interoperability Meets Accountability: How Data Interoperability and Experiential Quality Influence Malpractice Lawsuits
Authors: Sukrit Pal, David E. Cantor, Anand Nair
Abstract: A persistent challenge that many patients continue to face is substandard care including errors in their medical records (Sharma et al., 2019). To address this situation, health information exchanges (HIE) have been established to seamlessly share patient data across organizations. In this study, we examine whether policy-driven support for data interoperability—operationalized through health information exchange (HIE) systems—is associated with increased malpractice liability. Drawing on the empowerment literature, we argue that greater operational transparency enabled by data sharing may empower patients to scrutinize care quality, thereby elevating the risk of litigation. Using an eight-year panel data set covering 952 U.S. hospitals from 2010 to 2017 and over 24,000 malpractice case filings, we find that HIE adoption is associated with a statistically significant 10.5% increase in malpractice lawsuits. However, this effect is moderated by hospitals’ experiential quality, as measured by patient-reported experiences of communication, empathy, and responsiveness. In hospitals with high experiential quality, the effect of HIE adoption on malpractice lawsuits is reduced by 20.4%, suggesting that positive patient interactions can reduce the legal risks associated with HIE adoption. Our findings highlight a critical trade-off. While data interoperability improves operational coordination and patient engagement, it can also elevate legal exposure. This research contributes to the operations management and public policy literature by reframing interoperability not just as a backend coordination tool but also as a patient-facing technological development with reputational and legal implications.

Title: Participation Governance in Consumer and AI Co-creation: Whether to Intervene and How to Design It
Authors: Mengxia Zhang, Brian Rongqing Han, Tianshu Sun, Lan Luo, Joseph M. Golden
Abstract: Artificial intelligence reshapes digital mass customization by altering the structure of consumer co-creation. When consumers start from a draft generated by artificial intelligence rather than a blank canvas, outcomes are jointly determined by two stages: whether consumers initiate co-creation and, conditional on participation, how much refinement effort they exert. This separation makes participation a governable design margin—an issue that is largely muted in traditional blank-canvas customization, where participation and effort are tightly bundled. Partnering with a leading United States online retailer of personalized photo products, we study whether and how firm interventions at the participation stage shape downstream purchase outcomes. We develop a two-stage model in which, relative to a baseline with organic participation, a nudge lowers start-up frictions and expands voluntary entry, whereas a mandate serves as a strong boundary-case intervention that guarantees entry but can weaken how participation translates into purchase, generating a reach–efficiency trade-off. We examine these predictions in two randomized experiments. In Study 1, a light-touch nudge increases participation by 5.98 percentage points and raises revenue and order frequency. The evidence is consistent with gains arising primarily through expanded entry into consumer co-creation with artificial intelligence. In Study 2, mandates increase participation relative to nudges, but we find no clear evidence of additional gains in purchase or revisit intentions. Instead, mandates increase low-value participation, in which consumers exert minimal effort and report low purchase intention. Together, these findings show that in mass customization enabled by artificial intelligence, participation governance is a consequential design choice: firms must consider not only how many consumers initiate co-creation, but also whether the participation they induce creates downstream value.

Title: Harnessing Renewable Portfolio Standards for Sustainable Futures: An Empirical Examination of Spillover Effects
Authors: Chunjie Zhao, Anqi Wu, Ramanathan Subramanyam
Abstract: Given the importance of managing industrial energy consumption, setting standards and implementing policies that encourage renewable energy use is crucial for incentivizing sustainable firm practices. Public policy designs must align closely with firms’ environmental policies to help mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and support a sustainable future. While research on policy impacts on firm environmental performance and the supply chain's role in sustainability is growing, a critical, understudied effect is the spillover of government rules to supply chain partners and peer firms, especially those outside the direct purview of environmental regulations. This paper presents a novel approach that integrates data from the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and the Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS). The latter refers to state-driven initiatives that incentivize electricity consumption from eligible renewable resources. We examine the causal effects of state-level policies on firm-level GHG emission intensity, with particular emphasis on the spillover effects of policies on unregulated firms across markets. We break down emission intensity into Scope 1 and Scope 2 and capture facility-level data to analyze spillover effects in granular detail. Using a staggered difference-in-differences methodology, our analysis finds a promising negative association between RPS introduction and GHG emission intensity among unregulated firms across industries. Interestingly, firms headquartered in states with more conservative initial targets during RPS adoption and progressive, milestone-based implementation strategies have significantly lower GHG emission intensity than those headquartered in states with more aggressive initial targets or long-term absolute targets. Our findings have significant implications for developing environmental regulations and public policies aimed at reducing GHG emission intensity.

Title: What Drives Physician Efficiency? Evidence from Emergency Department Operations
Authors: Raha Imanirad, Soroush Saghafian, Stephen J. Traub, Nicole R. Hodgson
Abstract: Emergency department (ED) physicians play a critical role in healthcare, serving on the frontline of acute care delivery. Yet increasing demand, resource constraints, and growing patient complexity pose significant challenges to physician efficiency. In this study, we investigate the determinants of ED physician efficiency using a multi-stage framework. First, we apply Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) to measure individual physician efficiency based on data from 110,325 patient visits at a leading U.S. hospital. Second, we use a Tobit regression model to analyze how physician experience, shift familiarity, and patient severity influence physician efficiency. Third, we conduct comprehensive robustness checks, including omitted variable bias sensitivity analyses, permutation tests, and machine learning-based classification analyses, to address concerns regarding endogeneity and potential model misspecification. Our results show that physician efficiency increases with experience at a diminishing rate. Efficiency also varies with shift familiarity, with the estimated association weakening as physician experience increases. In addition, higher patient severity is associated with lower physician efficiency, consistent with the greater resource demands of caring for more clinically complex patients. This negative association is attenuated for more experienced physicians, suggesting that experienced physicians are better able to maintain efficiency when managing more demanding clinical conditions. Our findings offer actionable recommendations for improving ED operations. Staffing strategies that assign relatively more experienced physicians to higher-severity patients may help maintain physician efficiency, while shift familiarity may inform a scheduling strategy that emphasizes greater scheduling consistency for relatively less experienced physicians and greater flexibility for relatively more experienced physicians. Simulation results further illustrate the potential reductions in physician resource use associated with these strategies. Together, these findings highlight the value of evidence-based physician staffing and scheduling to improve physician efficiency in EDs.

Title: “Generate” the Future of Work through AI: Empirical Evidence from Online Labor Markets
Authors: Jin Liu, Xingchen Xu, Xi Nan, Yongjun Li, Yong Tan
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China School of Management, Department of Management Science, Hefei, Anhui, China; University of Washington, Information Systems and Operations Management, Seattle, Washington, 98195-0005, United States; University of Washington, Michael G. Foster School of Business, Seattle, Washington, 98195, United States; USTC, management science, Hefei, 230026, China; University of Washington, Michael G. Foster School of Business, Seattle, Washington, 98195-3200, United States
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based generative AI systems are general-purpose tools capable of augmenting or even automating a wide range of job functions, positioning them to reshape labor market dynamics. However, predicting their precise impact a priori is challenging, given AI’s simultaneous effects on both demand and supply, as well as the strategic responses of market participants. Leveraging an extensive dataset from a leading online labor platform, we document a pronounced displacement effect and an overall contraction in submarkets where required skills closely align with core LLM functionalities. Although demand and supply both decline, the reduction in supply is comparatively smaller, thereby intensifying competition among freelancers. Notably, further analysis shows that this heightened competition is especially pronounced in programming-intensive submarkets. This pattern is attributed to skill-transition effects: by lowering the human-capital barrier to programming, ChatGPT enables incumbent freelancers to enter programming tasks. Moreover, these transitions are not homogeneous, with high-skilled freelancers contributing disproportionately to the shift. Our findings illuminate the multifaceted impacts of general-purpose AI on labor markets, highlighting not only the displacement of certain occupations but also the inducement of skill transitions within the labor supply. These insights offer practical implications for policymakers, platform operators, and workers.

Title: Campaigns That Click: Unleashing the Power of Push Notifications on Mobile Apps
Authors: Zhuping Liu, Bicheng Yang, Subodha Kumar
Affiliations: Baruch College Zicklin School of Business, Marketing and International Business, New York, New York, United States; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Faculty of Business, management and marketing, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Temple University, Supply Chain, Information Systems, Marketing, and Statistics, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States
Abstract: As mobile apps increasingly mediate digital engagement, push notifications have emerged as a key tool for directing user attention, yet systematic evidence on their behavioral and ecosystem-level effects remains limited. Using data from over 200 push campaigns and 60 million user-campaign observations on a leading U.S. mobile-offer marketplace, we combine large-scale observational analyses with controlled experiments to study how push notifications shape user engagement. We find that push notifications significantly increase same-day click-throughs to advertised merchants, with substantial heterogeneity across merchant characteristics, user characteristics, message design, and delivery timing. Beyond focal-merchant responses, notifications are associated with increased engagement with non-advertised merchants both within and across categories, suggesting that push notifications reshape attention across the marketplace ecosystem. Both the large-scale empirical analysis and controlled experiments yield evidence consistent with two complementary mechanisms—content-driven processing of notification information and reminder-based attention activation. The results also identify attentional saturation as a key boundary condition—repeated exposure produces diminishing responsiveness and may even reduce engagement at high notification frequencies. These findings position push notifications as a mobile-native attention-allocation lever that platforms can strategically deploy, while underscoring the need to balance engagement gains against user fatigue and attention costs.

Title: Mobile Location-based Recommendation Systems and Local Businesses: Evidence from the Restaurant Industry
Authors: Jin Soo Han, Gunwoong Lee, Keongtae Kim
Affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology College of Business, IT Management, Seoul, Korea (the Republic of); Korea University, Management Information Systems, Seongbuk-gu, Seoul, Korea (the Republic of); Chinese University of Hong Kong, Decisions, Operations and Technology, Shatin, Hong Kong
Abstract: We investigate the impact of mobile location-based recommendation systems (MLBRS) on the performance of local businesses. Leveraging a comprehensive dataset of 16,720 restaurants and quasi-experimental variation generated by the official launch of a leading MLBRS, we employ a 2-Stage Least Squares instrumental-variable framework to estimate the effect of algorithmic exposure on consumer engagement. Our analysis reveals that a 1% increase in exposure is associated with a 0.078% increase in clicks; separately, a 1% increase in clicks is associated with a 0.053% increase in visit intentions. Importantly, the estimated exposure effect is larger for geographically disadvantaged restaurants, but primarily at the discovery stage (clicks). This pattern highlights a boundary condition of MLBRS: algorithmic visibility can aid, but it does not by itself resolve the uncertainty involved in acting on a recommendation. Downstream conversion is stronger when restaurants provide richer digital information and reputation signals, including consumer reviews and owner-curated information such as photos and menus. Auxiliary credit-card sales data from a restricted Seoul subsample provide consistent evidence of a positive association between algorithmic exposure and revenue, suggesting that MLBRS can shape the connection of online recommendations to offline economic outcomes.

Title: Looking Under the Hood of Commodity Currency Predictability
Authors: Alexandre Jeanneret, Valeri Sokolovski
Affiliations: School of Banking and Finance, UNSW Business School, Kensington, New South Wales 2033, Australia; Alberta School of Business, University of Alberta, Edmonton AB T6G 2R3, Canada
Abstract: This paper revisits the exchange rate predictability of commodity currencies through the lens of market efficiency. Focusing on currencies with strong contemporaneous exposure to commodity prices, we show that changes in country-specific commodity export or import prices predict exchange rate fluctuations both in sample and out of sample. We establish four empirical facts: (i) the sign of the predictive relationship runs counter to standard risk-based explanations; (ii) predictability is concentrated at short horizons; (iii) predictability is driven by a small set of thinly traded currencies; and (iv) even sophisticated speculative traders adjust positions sluggishly in response to commodity price shocks in these currencies. Together, these findings suggest that predictability arises from the slow incorporation of information in less actively traded currencies, which is likely due to liquidity and position-building constraints, rather than from compensation for risk. The results also clarify the sources of commodity-based predictability in carry trade returns. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Title: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
Authors: Øystein Foros, Hans Jarle Kind, Greg Shaffer
Affiliations: Norwegian School of Economics (NHH), 5045 Bergen, Norway; and CESifo, 81679 Munich, Germany; University of Rochester, Rochester, New York 14627
Abstract: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter. Second, when fixed payments arise, they often flow from suppliers to retailers (slotting fees) rather than the reverse. We develop and analyze a model of multilateral bargaining in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers to explain these patterns. The key mechanism is a trade-off between two distortions: under linear contracts, wholesale prices reflect bargaining power and can be either above or below the channel-profit-maximizing level, whereas under two-part tariffs, wholesale prices are set to maximize bilateral surplus independently of bargaining power but are systematically too low from an overall channel perspective because of rent shifting across relationships. As a result, neither contractual form uniformly dominates; instead, relative performance depends on how bargaining shapes gains from trade across firms. When bargaining leads to slotting fees, two-part tariffs yield higher channel profits than linear contracts, whereas when it would imply payments from retailers to suppliers, linear contracts may perform better. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of linear contracts alongside two-part tariffs, the direction of fixed payments, and the conditions under which each contractual form is likely to arise. This paper was accepted by Miguel Villas-Boas, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03426 .
