Title: Optimize-via-Estimate: How to Make Finite-Sample Corrections for Sampling Uncertainty in Data-Driven Optimization
Authors: Gar Goei Loke, Taozeng Zhu, Ruiting Zuo
Affiliations: Durham University Business School, Department of Management and Marketing, Durham, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Dongbei University of Finance and Economics, Institute of Supply Chain Analytics, Dalian, China; National University of Singapore, Analytics & Operations, Singapore, Singapore
Abstract: We propose a novel procedure for correcting for the effects of sampling and parameter uncertainty in data-driven convex optimization. We consider the data-driven setting wherein the distribution lies in a parametric family with unknown parameter. The decision-maker possesses a historical data set, from which solves a prescriptive solution as a function mapping such a data set to decisions, and measures its out-of-sample performance as an average over data sets of the same size under the sampling distribution. As the parameter is unknown to the decision-maker, we argue that this problem is ill-defined and further prove that there cannot exist solutions generalizably optimal over all parameters. As such, we formulate the problem as a weighted multi-criteria optimization with weights defined by a density (termed ‘prior’) over the uncertain parameter, and call its optimal solution prior optimal. We prove that sufficient conditions for prior optimality reduces to functions of the sufficient statistic of the parametric family, and this function can be solved as a point-wise optima of a corrected function of the original objective, with terms accounting for parameter uncertainty and sampling uncertainty respectively. The correction for sampling interpretation is verified by a close to (but not) zero ex-ante regret against a perfect information oracle in numerical illustrations on the newsvendor and portfolio optimization problems.

Title: Real-Time Solution of Quadratic Optimization Problems with Banded Matrices and Indicator Variables
Authors: Andres Gomez, Shaoning Han, Leonardo Lozano
Affiliations: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, 90089, United States; University of Southern California, The Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Los Angeles, California, 90089-0001, United States; University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio, United States
Abstract: We consider mixed-integer quadratic optimization problems with banded matrices and indicator variables. These problems arise pervasively in statistical inference problems with time-series data, where the banded matrix captures the temporal relationship of the underlying process. In particular, the problem studied arises in monitoring problems, where the decision-maker wants to detect changes or anomalies. We propose to solve these problems using decision diagrams. In particular we show how to exploit the temporal dependencies to construct exact and approximate decision diagrams. For problems over matrices with bandwidth equal to one, the proposed method runs in polynomial time. Moreover, if the bandwidth and condition number of the matrix is fixed, then we show that the proposed method can be modified to run into an additive approximation scheme. We also describe how to construct the convex hull of the set under study from the decision diagrams, and how to deploy the method online to solve the problems via a shortest path algorithm. Computational experiments show that, for problems with bandwidths less or equal than three, our proposed algorithm compares favorably to a state-of-the-art off-the-shelf solver in the offline setting, and that we are able to solve problems in milliseconds for the online setting.

Title: Online Allocation with Heterogeneous Supply and Minimum Workload Guarantees
Authors: Garud Iyengar, Raghav Singal
Affiliations: Department of IEOR, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027; Tuck School of Business, Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire 03755

Title: On the Maximization of Long-Run Conditional Value-at-Risk for Markov Decision Processes
Authors: Li Xia, Zhihui Yu, Haoran Wu
Affiliations: School of Business, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou 510275, China
Abstract: Optimizing Risk-Seeking Sequential Decisions via Conditional Value-at-Risk Decision makers may exhibit risk-seeking preferences in finance, energy operations, and stochastic resource management, yet corresponding Markov decision process (MDP) theories remain underdeveloped. In this paper, “On the Maximization of Long-Run CVaR for Markov Decision Processes,” Xia, Yu, and Wu investigate infinite-horizon MDPs maximizing long-run conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) for instantaneous rewards. They prove optimality for stationary randomized policies and show deterministic policies may fail; an optimal policy randomizes over at most two actions. By converting the original problem into a minimax saddle point formulation, the authors develop solvable linear programming and globally convergent gradient descent algorithms. Results are further extended to joint mean-CVaR optimization and validated on real-world microgrid scheduling data. This work fills gaps for risk-seeking MDPs and delivers practical computation tools for tail-oriented sequential decision making.

Title: Information Transparency, Choice Confidence, and Customer Retention: Field and Laboratory Evidence from Markets for Credence Goods
Authors: Zhi (Aaron) Cheng, Ting Li, Paul A. Pavlou
Affiliations: Department of Management, London School of Economics, London WC2A 2AE, United Kingdom; Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University, Rotterdam 3062 PA, Netherlands; University of Miami Business School, Miami, Florida 33146
Abstract: How does information transparency affect customer retention in markets where quality is difficult to verify? Conventional wisdom suggests that transparency intensifies price competition and increases customer churn. We challenge this view by showing that acquisition-stage transparency can strengthen retention in markets for credence goods characterized by delayed feedback and persistent uncertainty, where customers revisit their decisions without clear quality signals. We develop a transparency-confidence-retention framework, in which transparency at acquisition builds choice confidence, a psychological switching cost that anchors customers to their initial decisions. Using 83,835 auto insurance contracts from a European insurer and multiple identification strategies, we find that customers acquired through transparent channels are 4.6%–11.8% less likely to churn than those acquired through less transparent channels. A randomized, controlled experiment with 1,515 participants shows that transparency reduces customer churn primarily by strengthening choice confidence rather than increasing conventional switching costs, such as brand trust or product fit. Decomposing transparency into attribute, comparative, and evaluative dimensions reveals that evaluative transparency exerts the strongest influence. Analyses of boundary conditions indicate that the retention effect of transparency is amplified when public and private signals remain congruent with earlier informational cues. These findings reconceptualize transparency as a relational mechanism that fosters decisional assurance and stabilizes retention under quality uncertainty. Title: From Winning to Giving: The Effect of Gold Medals in Crowdsourcing Contests
Authors: Shan Liu, Fan Zhang, Jing Wang, Baojun Gao
Affiliations: School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China; Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics, and Operations Management, School of Business and Management, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China; Business School of Science and Technology, Wuhan University, Wuhan 430072, China
Abstract: We examine how users respond to winning symbolic awards in online crowdsourcing contests. Our setting is a machine learning competition platform that grants symbolic medals to recognize participants’ contest achievements. Employing a regression discontinuity design, we find that gold medal winners participate less in subsequent contests but engage more in prosocial activities, evidenced by a greater volume and length of posts, as well as more substantial and frequent code contributions. In contrast, bronze and silver medals do not seem to exert a significant influence on recipients’ subsequent behaviors. Drawing on self-determination theory and the needs-as-motives hypothesis, we provide evidence that need-driven goal shifting plays an important role in driving the dual effects of gold medals—diminished contest participation but enhanced prosocial contributions. Further analyses reveal that winners with previous competition medals are more likely to favor contributing content over competing again, whereas winners with more prior contribution medals are less inclined to further increase contributions. Moreover, team winners exhibit a lower tendency than solo winners to shift their efforts from competition to contribution. We add to the symbolic awards literature by uncovering a novel goal-shifting effect induced by contest medals, where award receipt redirects user effort from the focal rewarded domain to other forms of platform engagement. Title: From Bytes to Bites: Examining the Online and Offline Spillover Impacts of Online Food Delivery Platform Subscriptions
Authors: Jaeho Myeong, Yongjin Park, Francis Joseph Costello, Keongtae Kim, Jae-Hyeon Ahn
Affiliations: College of Business and Economics, Hanyang University ERICA, Ansan 15588, Republic of Korea; College of Business, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Nova School of Business and Economics, Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, Campus de Carcavelos, 2775-405 Carcavelos, Portugal; Chinese University of Hong Kong Business School, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; College of Business, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Seoul 02455, Republic of Korea; and Seoul Business School, Seoul School of Integrated Sciences & Technologies (aSSIST) University, Seoul 03767, Republic of Korea
Abstract: With the rapid expansion of online food delivery (OFD) platforms, subscription models have emerged as a strategic tool to retain users and shape consumption behavior. Despite their growing prevalence, the broader impacts of these subscriptions—both within the OFD sector and across downstream consumer activities—remain underexplored. Leveraging a difference-in-differences approach and a large-scale individual-level transaction data set, we identify a significant shift in consumption from a competing platform to the focal platform following the introduction of a subscription service. This shift did not result in cannibalization; instead, overall food consumption within the OFD market increased. Geospatial analysis shows that subscribers were more likely to engage in offline spillovers, including increased local dining and activity in nearby noncompeting economic sectors. These patterns suggest that subscriptions in physical services, like OFD, not only reshape digital engagement, but also, they influence consumer mobility and stimulate localized economic ecosystems. Mechanistic testing supports the interpretation that these effects are driven by increased variety-seeking behavior for offline restaurants that predominantly serve non-OFD cuisines within a proximal location, suggesting that such behavior is constrained by transportation costs. Overall, this study offers novel insights into how subscription models in physical service platforms can expand market demand, foster crosschannel engagement, and generate positive spillovers in adjacent sectors. The findings offer actionable guidance for platform designers and policymakers to enhance consumer welfare and support local economic vitality. They also provide new evidence for restaurants that additional platform usage costs may be offset by latent economic benefits from heightened consumer engagement. This paper was accepted by D. J. Title: Why Zoning Is Too Restrictive
Authors: Jack Favilukis, Jaehee Song
Affiliations: Sauder School of Business, The University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia V6T 1Z2, Canada; Leeds School of Business, University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado 80309
Abstract: Economists estimate that zoning regulations raise house prices, lower productivity, and reduce aggregate welfare, yet regulations remain widespread. We develop and solve a model in which fragmented zoning authority leads to overly strict regulations: Homeowners impose stricter regulations to mitigate local congestion but fail to internalize the broader impact on metro-wide affordability. Empirically, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of local governments explains 12% of the variation in zoning restrictiveness. Using an instrument based on 19th-century municipal fragmentation, we show that greater fragmentation leads to stricter zoning and higher housing costs. These findings suggest that centralizing zoning decisions could alleviate housing affordability challenges. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Title: The Effects of Search Interface on Consumer Preferences: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
Authors: Jia Liu, Olivier Toubia
Affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Business School, Marketing, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Columbia University, Columbia Business School, New York, New York, 10025, United States
Abstract: While structured search interfaces—such as filters and sorting tools—help consumers reduce search frictions on digital platforms, they also shape how consumers encounter product information during search. This paper studies how search interface design influences revealed preferences and market outcomes. We develop a theoretical framework linking interface design to attribute preferences through salience reallocation and information-based preference updating. The framework generates two predictions that can be formally derived: restricting faceted filters reduces the concentration of attribute importance weights (i.e., preference dispersion) and increases the diversity of products chosen (i.e., choice diversity). We test these predictions using a randomized, incentive-aligned online experiment in which 1,200 participants searched for wireless headphones on a custom-built e-commerce platform. Restricting filters led consumers to explore more broadly and resulted in more evenly distributed attribute importance weights and more diverse, higher-priced product choices. Mediation analysis further suggests that increased exploration was associated with shifts in attribute preferences. Our findings demonstrate that search interface design can construct, rather than merely reveal, consumer preferences.

Title: Share Issues vs. Share Repurchases
Authors: Philip Bond, Yue Yuan, Hongda Zhong
Affiliations: Foster School of Business, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195; and Finance Theory Group, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; Finance Theory Group, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; and School of Management and Department of Economics, University College London, London E14 5AA, United Kingdom; and University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas 75080; and The Centre for Economic Policy Research, London, EC1R 5HL, United Kingdom
Abstract: Almost all firms repurchase shares through open-market repurchase programs. In contrast, issue methods are more diverse; at-the-market offerings, analogous to open-market repurchases, and seasoned equity offerings, analogous to rarely used tender-offer repurchases, are both used by significant fractions of firms. Furthermore, average seasoned equity offerings are larger than at-the-market offerings. We show that this asymmetry in the diversity of transaction methods in issuances and repurchases and the size-method relation in issuances are natural consequences of the single informational friction of a firm having superior information to investors. Moreover, although this friction always leads firms to issue inefficiently little, it leads firms to repurchase too little if they maximize long-term shareholder value but too much if the primary goal is to boost short-term share prices. Title: Cross-Cluster Referrals and Subsidy Schemes in Multi-Cluster Healthcare Systems
Authors: Liming Liu, Weixin Shang, Xiuli Chao, Shaohui Zheng
Affiliations: Lingnan University, Faculty of Business, Hong Kong; University of Michigan, Dept. of Industrial & Operations Engineering, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, School of Business and Management, Hong Kong
Abstract: Problem definition: Excessive and highly variable waiting times for specialty services are a long-standing problem for public healthcare systems. Healthcare authorities in some jurisdictions have begun to experiment with schemes to improve system performance, including cross-cluster referrals which allow patients to switch from their home cluster to other clusters with shorter waiting times, and opt-out subsidies which help patients seeking services from private providers outside the public system. However, few studies in the literature have examined the structure of the problem or offered analytical insights to the design of such schemes. Methodology/results: We construct a multi-cluster service network model to study optimal routing policies under both individual and system optimization. We define externalities in a network setting and establish their properties, and further identify conditions under which referrals are effective or counterproductive in reducing system costs. We also show that lowering the switching cost could inadvertently degrade overall system performance. In contrast to the classic result for single-cluster systems (e.g. Naor 1969), our analysis of opt-out and switching incentives reveals that fixed subsidies generally cannot fully coordinate a multi-cluster system due to the cross-cluster effect of externalities. However, they can effectively reduce system costs in wide ranges of system parameter values. We further show that dynamic (state-dependent) subsidies can achieve perfect alignment between individual and system optimization. Managerial implications: Our study suggests that cross-cluster referrals are effective when there is a substantial workload imbalance but without excessive system congestion. They should be implemented with proper operational control: referrals should be promoted when the workload imbalance is high, but discouraged when the overall system workload is very high while the imbalance is insubstantial. Furthermore, fixed opt-out and switching subsidies can effectively improve system performance under different demand conditions and should be applied strategically: focusing on switching subsidies when the system workload is moderate and the imbalance is substantial, but shifting the focus to opt-out subsidies when the overall system workload is high.

Title: A Decision-Support Framework for Food Bank Operations: Overcoming Waste and Uncertainty in Food Distribution
Authors: Xianjia Gao, Xin Chen
Affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Gies College of Business, Urbana, Illinois, United States; Georgia Institute of Technology, H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Atlanta, Georgia, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: Food banks face the complex operational challenge of allocating uncertain and per- ishable food donations to maximize community benefit. This requires navigating difficult trade-offs between effectiveness (delivering nutritious and fresh food relative to need), efficiency (maximizing food distributed and minimizing waste), and equity (ensuring fair distribution), a task for which traditional myopic poli- cies are often ill-equipped. Our research addresses how food banks can design practical, forward-looking allocation strategies in this dynamic and challenging environment. Methodology/results: We develop a comprehensive dynamic programming framework to model the food bank allocation problem. From this, we derive two practical and implementable policies: a simple, static Scaled Fluid (SF) policy and an adaptive Re-Optimized (ReOPT) policy. We provide rigorous theoretical proofs that both policies are asymptotically optimal. Furthermore, extensive simulations using both synthetic and real data show that our proposed strategies yield significant utility gains. Managerial implications: This research provides food bank man- agers and decision-makers with theoretically sound and empirically validated tools to improve their opera- tions. Our framework offers a clear path to enhance the impact and sustainability of food distribution efforts, enabling organizations to better serve their communities by making more efficient, effective, and equitable decisions with the resources they have.

Title: Humanitarian Aid Management under Corruptible Distribution and Oversight Agents
Authors: Paola Martin, Owen Q. Wu, Larysa Yakymova
Affiliations: Indiana University, ODT, Bloomington, Indiana, United States; Indiana University Bloomington Kelley School of Business, Department of Operations & Decision Technologies, Bloomington, Indiana, United States; Yuriy Fedkovych Chernivtsi National University, Department of Economic and Mathematical Modelling, Cernivici, Černìvec′kа, Ukraine
Abstract: Problem Definition: In many crisis contexts, such as armed conflicts, natural disasters, or refugee emergencies, one of the most pressing challenges is to regulate the delivery of humanitarian aid to the final beneficiaries in the presence of both corruptible agents (those responsible for delivering aid) and corruptible inspectors (who may be bribed not to report uncovered misappropriations). Strengthening anti-corruption efforts by hiring more inspectors and/or rewarding inspectors’ truthful reporting can reduce corruption but draws on the finite humanitarian aid financing, reducing the aid delivered to the beneficiaries. Methodology/Results: We develop a three-stage game-theoretic model in which a government agency chooses inspection intensity and the reward rate for inspectors’ truthful reporting, managers decide how much aid to misappropriate, and inspectors decide whether to report detected misconduct or accept a bribe to conceal misappropriation. The government agency aims to maximize the amount of humanitarian aid reaching the beneficiaries. We find that the role of inspectors depends on the financing available. When the financing is low, inspectors serve to detect misconduct; when the financing is sufficiently high, inspectors also affect managers' behavior and deter misappropriation. The reward can also serve two purposes. It can either induce truthful reporting and eliminate bribery, or increase the bribe that managers must pay, thereby reducing their incentive to misappropriate. We characterize the impact of key parameters on the optimal anti-corruption levers. Managerial Implications: Our results provide guidance for agencies and donors on how to balance aid provision with anti-corruption measures, and how to adjust inspection intensity and incentive for truthful reporting to maximize the amount of aid reaching its intended recipients. As financing changes, resources should be allocated toward adjusting inspection intensity. In contrast, the reward rate for truthful reporting should be calibrated to the enforcement environment, and not be mechanically increased with the amount of financing.

Title: Improving operational performance through boarding time slack: Evidence from the U.S. airline industry
Authors: Chandrasekhar Manchiraju, Ashutosh Bhave, Milind G Sohoni
Affiliations: Michigan State University; University of Arkansas; The State University of New York
Abstract: Flight delays have a significant impact on airlines, passengers, and the U.S. economy. Airlines also use flight on-time performance (OTP)—a metric based on the proportion of delayed flights—to attract travelers by demonstrating service reliability. It is well established that adding buffers to flight time and ground time improves on-time arrivals. However, such buffers can impose significant costs. The flight and ground times comprise multiple activities, and prior research has primarily focused on studying the impact of aggregate buffers. In this article, we study the impact of increasing the buffer of a critical ground time activity, namely boarding time, potentially without increasing the aggregate ground time buffer, on flight delays. To do so, we use the context of Delta Air Lines’ recent policy changes wherein the airline increased the boarding time for domestic narrow-body flights by 5 minutes and started compensating flight attendants for pre-flight boarding. Using a difference-in-difference-in-differences framework, we analyze and quantify the impact of these policies on Delta’s flight delays. Our findings indicate a significant reduction in departure delays following the policy changes, with increased boarding time playing a critical role in improving on-time departures. Our analysis finds no evidence that boarding compensation contributed to the improvement in on-time departures. We show that the increase in boarding time can improve the likelihood of on-time departures, potentially without requiring additional total ground time or incurring additional scheduling costs. We observe that the benefit is more pronounced for longer flights, busier routes, and later departures in the day. Airlines are often criticized for relying on costly, ad hoc schedule buffering to improve OTP. However, our results demonstrate that carefully planning buffer time for critical activities can significantly improve operational performance.

Title: Assortment Optimization Given Basket Shopping Behavior Using the Ising Model
Authors: Andrey Vasilyev, Sebastian Maier, Ralf W. Seifert
Abstract: In markets where customers tend to purchase baskets of products rather than single products, assortment optimization is a major challenge for retailers. Removing a product from a retailer's assortment can result in a severe drop in aggregate demand if this product is a complement to other products. Therefore, accounting for the complementarity effect is essential when making assortment decisions. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework designed to address this problem. We model customers' choices using the binary Ising model, which is a special case of a Markov random field. This model captures pairwise demand dependencies as well as the individual attractiveness of each product, with binary variables indicating whether products are included in the purchased basket. For estimation, we utilize existing methods developed for the spin formulation of the Ising model and then apply a parameter transformation to express the fitted model in the binary form used for assortment optimization. We show that the assortment optimization problem under the Ising model is NP-hard. We also provide multiple theoretical insights into the structure of the optimal assortments based on the graphical representation of the Ising model, and propose several heuristic algorithms that can be used to obtain high-quality solutions to the assortment optimization problem. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the developed simulated annealing procedure leads to an expected profit gain of 15% compared to offering an unoptimized assortment (where all products are included) and around 5% compared to using a revenue-ordered heuristic algorithm.

Title: Technology-Mediated Services in Health Care: Evaluating Telehealth Delivery Models for Underserved Populations
Authors: Kyuyeon (Jenny) Rhee, Xiao Liu, Suparerk Lekwijit, Pei-Yu Chen
Affiliations: Arizona State University, Information Systems, Tempe, Arizona, United States; Arizona State University W P Carey School of Business, Information Systems, Tempe, Arizona, United States
Abstract: This study examines how telehealth delivery models are associated with access to care and protocol adherence in underserved populations. While prior research reports mixed evidence on telehealth’s effectiveness, we argue that these inconsistencies arise because telehealth is not a single intervention but is implemented through distinct service configurations that address different barriers. Drawing on the theoretical framework of digital economics, we conceptualize telehealth as a technology-mediated service that can alter key economic frictions, including search and verification, transportation, tracking, and setup costs. We focus on two widely adopted models—specialist-facilitated telehealth and remote telehealth—and theorize that each addresses different subsets of these frictions, leading to distinct effects on care access and protocol adherence across settings. Using panel data from U.S. Community Health Centers on mental health services, we document three findings. First, adoption of the specialist-facilitated model is associated with increased access to mental health care, particularly in areas with greater clinical need. Second, remote telehealth is not associated with increased access on average but is associated with higher adherence to standardized depression screening and follow-up protocols. These effects are consistent with improvements in screening and documentation processes rather than increases in utilization. Third, the estimated effects of both models vary across local cost environments. The access effects of specialist-facilitated telehealth are larger in areas where search and verification frictions are greater. In contrast, the effects of remote telehealth are attenuated where patient-side setup costs are high but are larger where transportation barriers and documentation frictions are greater. These findings advance a model-specific perspective on telehealth’s effects, extend the digital economics framework to technology-mediated services, and provide evidence that the estimated effects of digital health interventions vary with how delivery models interact with underlying cost environments.

Title: Does Private Equity Hurt or Improve Healthcare Value? New Evidence and Mechanisms
Authors: Minghong Yuan, Wen Wen, Indranil Roy Bardhan
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, Information Risk and Operations Management, Austin, Texas, United States; The University of Texas at Austin, McCombs School of Business, Austin, Texas, United States; The University of Texas at Austin, Information, Risk & Operations Management, Austin, Texas, United States
Abstract: What is the impact of private equity (PE) ownership on healthcare value? Does PE ownership reduce healthcare value, and if so, can its effect be mitigated using health information technologies (IT)? Given the significant investments by PE firms in the healthcare sector in recent years, it is increasingly important for stakeholders, including policy makers, care providers, and patients, to understand their likely impact and whether PE ownership is aligned with their interests. Because PE firms seek to improve efficiency and generate short-term financial returns, the cost-cutting strategies used to achieve these goals may come at the expense of care quality, leading to competing hypotheses on the impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. We argue that IT-enabled health information sharing capabilities can help PE-owned hospitals to better manage this cost-quality tension and achieve higher healthcare value. Using a staggered difference-in-differences approach and data from US hospitals from 2008 to 2020, we estimate changes in healthcare value following PE acquisition and ownership. Overall, we find that PE ownership of hospitals reduces healthcare value. This decline is partially driven by reduction in clinical staffing following PE ownership. We further find that pre-existing, hospital health information sharing capabilities mitigate the negative impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. Specifically, such capabilities can strengthen the effect of PE ownership on cost reduction and, at the same time, mitigate PE-induced, care quality deterioration. Our results highlight the critical role of common data standards needed to promote IT-enabled information sharing between healthcare providers, which, in turn, can align the incentives of PE firms with the goals of value-based care.

Title: The Motivational Paradox: How Aspirational-Goal Communications Influence Sales Performance and Information Acquisition
Authors: Doug J. Chung, Dongkyu Chang
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, Marketing, Austin, Texas, United States; City University of Hong Kong, Economics and Finance, Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong
Abstract: This study examines how aspirational-goal communications influence sales agents’ performance and information-seeking behavior. In a field experiment across 100 stores in Sweden, agents in the treatment group received daily personalized text messages with aspirational sales goals tailored to their prior performance. Results show that these communications increase sales performance, particularly among low-performing agents, primarily through higher unit sales. At the same time, they reduce agents’ willingness to monitor within-day sales progress—reflecting the ostrich effect—which can adversely affect performance. Information acquisition, in the form of sales-progress monitoring, typically aids effort provision, but aspirational-goal communications suppress such behavior, complicating performance management. These findings highlight the dual effects of aspirational-goal communications: while they enhance motivation, they may also prompt information avoidance. The study contributes to research on goal setting and sales management by clarifying the trade-offs in designing effective motivational and communication strategies.

Title: AI in Disguise—Quasi-Experimental Analysis of a Large-Scale Deployment of AI-Generated Ads
Authors: Yannick Exner, Jochen Hartmann, Ziqian Ding, Shunyuan Zhang, Oded Netzer
Affiliations: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Management, Munich, Germany; Technical University of Munich, Munchen, Germany; Carnegie Mellon University Tepper School of Business, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States; Harvard Business School, Marketing, Boston, Massachusetts, United States; Columbia University, Marketing, New York, New York, United States
Abstract: As Taboola prepared to launch its GenAI Ad Maker, a tool that lets advertisers create ad images within the platform, it faced a consequential question about whether AI-generated ad images would perform well with real consumers, and under what conditions. Working with Taboola, we construct a quasi-experimental comparison of 4,633 ‘sibling ads,’ meaning AI-generated and human-made images launched by the same advertisers, in identical campaign settings, at the same time. These ads span more than 369 million impressions and 2.5 million clicks. We do not find a detectable average click-through-rate disadvantage for AI-generated images relative to their human-made siblings. However, this average masks an important boundary condition: ads with AI-generated images outperform human-made ads when the AI images do not ‘look like AI.’ We identify key visual features influencing consumers’ perceptions of whether an ad looks AI-generated. While AI generates sharper, clearer, and less blurry images with larger faces, consumers associate these features with human-made ads. On the other hand, in line with consumers’ expectations, aesthetics, lower warmth, and intense color saturation in ads signal AI generation. These findings support Taboola’s roll-out communication, advertiser guidance, and continued refinement of the GenAI Ad Maker.

Title: Disagreement and Bond PEAD
Authors: Yoshio Nozawa, Yancheng Qiu, Yan Xiong
Affiliations: University of Toronto, UTSC Management, Toronto, Ontario M1C 1A4, Canada; The University of Sydney Business School, Sydney, New South Wales 2006, Australia; Faculty of Business and Economics, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
Abstract: This paper documents post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) in corporate bond prices using transaction data. We find a counterintuitive relationship between the drift and trading volume: PEAD is more pronounced for more heavily traded bonds than for less frequently traded bonds. Across markets, PEAD is observed for credit default swaps but not for stocks. We explain these findings using a unified model that incorporates both debt and equity trading, where investors possess private information about the underlying firm’s cash flows and may hold differing opinions. Our empirical evidence supports the model’s prediction that payoff structures and investor disagreement account for the distinct price dynamics across asset classes. Title: Conditional and Lenient Drug Approvals
Authors: Chenxi Xu, Giuseppe Lopomo, David Ridley, Peng Sun
Affiliations: Mitchell E. Daniels, Jr. School of Business, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana 47907; Fuqua School of Business, Duke University, Durham, North Carolina 27708
Abstract: Firms are often allowed to sell new drugs based on preliminary efficacy evidence, with final approval contingent on confirmatory testing. We characterize optimal approval policies for a government agency that maximizes consumer welfare while considering the firm’s incentives. We assume that firms have private information about testing costs and the government’s payoff depends on the drug’s expected efficacy. The optimal policy may include partial conditional approval for drugs with low expected efficacy, and leniency in granting final approval below conventional standards. Our calibration suggests these tools can generate hundreds of millions of dollars in annual social value. This paper was accepted by Martin Bichler, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Title: Gendered Effects of a Crisis-induced Work-from-Home Shock: A Time-Motion Study Using Digital Footprints
Authors: Kamalini Ramdas, Amalia Miller, Alp Sungu
Affiliations: London Business School, Management Science & Operations, London, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; University of Virginia, Economics, United States; University of Pennsylvania Wharton School, Operations, Information and Decisions Dept, Philadelphia, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: While organizations are adopting hybrid and even remote-first work schedules, the potentially gendered impact of work-from-home (WFH) on operational outcomes remains poorly understood. Methodology/results: To examine this question, we combine a crisis-induced shock (i.e., the Covid-19 lockdown) that forced a shift to WFH due to stay-at-home orders, with a novel methodology to gather contextualized digital trace data. We examine the online time allocation — akin to a time-motion study for white collars — of 1,094 individuals across various activities and industries, when in-person work related and leisure activities were abruptly curtailed by the pandemic, inducing a shift to home-based work and online activities. Analysis of over 30 million website visits reveals that overall, this crisis-induced WFH increased the time devoted to both work-related and leisure pursuits online. However, these gains are significantly larger for men, giving rise to new gender gaps. We observe notable disparities in online work and leisure activities, including on smartphones, suggesting that crisis-induced WFH reshapes workers’ daily activities differently across genders. These gender differences are amplified among parents — a pattern consistent with increased household obligations placing greater constraints on women’s ability to fully benefit from the flexibility offered by WFH. Furthermore, we observe a substantial relative decline in women’s job search activities after the WFH shock, also corroborated using a large, external dataset from a major online recruitment platform. Managerial implications: These results underscore how sudden WFH mandates as response to a major crisis can differentially affect women’s work, employment prospects and long-term career trajectories. Our findings call attention to the importance of factors outside of the office in determining the success of WFH arrangements. Even though WFH could lower facilities cost and carbon footprint and increase workers’ flexibility, gender-specific constraints — especially those related to household responsibilities — can produce uneven outcomes. These results highlight the need for organizations and policymakers to design WFH policies that effectively address gender disparities, particularly in environments where childcare and other domestic duties fall disproportionately on women.

Title: Operational Implications of Diagnostic Discrepancies: The Weigh-In of Focal and Related Physician Experience
Authors: Seokjun Youn, Yingchao Lan
Affiliations: University of Arizona, Management Information Systems, Tucson, Arizona, United States; University of Nebraska — Lincoln, Supply Chain Management and Analytics, Lincoln, Nebraska, United States
Abstract: Problem Definition: Diagnostic discrepancies, defined as mismatches between patients’ admitting and principal diagnoses, are common but heterogeneous claims-based markers. These discrepancies represent a misalignment in the diagnostic process, reflecting diagnostic updating, reprioritization, residual clinical complexity, documentation practices, or error, without establishing clinical preventability, and may signal latent operational burden in subsequent physician decision-making. We examine whether this retrospective operational flag identifies inpatient stays with larger adjusted resource-use differentials and whether those differentials vary with physician experience. Methodology/Results: Leveraging a patient-level dataset of 5.7 million emergency-department-origin inpatient stays from Florida hospitals, we examine the operational burden associated with diagnostic discrepancies, measured by total costs per hospitalization. Our results show that discrepancy-flagged inpatient stays have a 6.62% higher adjusted total cost after rich patient risk adjustment and high-dimensional fixed effects. The adjusted differential is smaller at higher focal experience (treating similar diagnoses) and larger at higher related experience (treating diverse diagnoses). The pattern remains qualitatively similar across alternative discrepancy definitions, richer diagnosis and service-line controls, risk-adjusted benchmarking, physician matching, alternative experience measures, and alternative samples. Exploratory analyses further show that flagged inpatient stays exhibit higher costs across multiple resource-use domains with varying intensity, higher diagnostic and procedural intensity, and longer adjusted time to first procedure. Managerial Implications: The discrepancy flag is most appropriately used for retrospective monitoring, benchmarking, and case-review triage, not as a direct measure of preventable error or as an automatic performance score. The physician experience patterns motivate prospective evaluation of assignment, consultation, training, and decision-support practices.

Title: Semibandit Learning for Monotone Stochastic Optimization
Authors: Rohan Ghuge, Zhengjia Zhuo, Arpit Agarwal, Viswanath Nagarajan
Affiliations: Department of Information, Risk, and Operations Management, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712; Department of Industrial and Operations Engineering, University of Michigan–Ann Arbor, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109; Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400076, India

Title: Evaluating the Impacts of Bundling on a Firm’s Product Demand and Operational Decisions
Authors: Shu-Jung Sunny Yang, Yingying Huang, Hsin Lu, Yuan-Hao Chu
Abstract: Firms use bundles to influence customer demand, but supplying those bundles often requires operational capacity that is shared across the portfolio. Changing the price, composition, or availability of one bundle can therefore trigger two reallocations: customers reallocate expenditure across bundles, and the firm reallocates operational capacity across the demand those bundles generate. We develop a data-driven framework that links these two decisions. Heterogeneous consumers choose discrete bundle quantities subject to a common budget, while the firm jointly chooses bundle prices and quantities subject to bundle-specific and shared-resource requirements. We estimate the demand and supply models from observed discrete decisions using Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo, retaining the integer structure in estimation and counterfactual analysis. We apply the framework to three empirical settings: public bike sharing, online retail, and theme-park services. The empirical analyses reveal several consequences of evaluating bundles as part of a portfolio. Customer value and profit contribution need not be aligned: a bundle that creates substantial customer value can make little or no incremental contribution to optimized profit, and removing some bundles can increase profit after the remaining portfolio is re-optimized. Price responses differ across bundles because discrete purchases adjust at different thresholds. A bundle's response to tighter shared-resource requirements depends on how its resource use changes the allocation of operational capacity elsewhere in the portfolio, rather than on its characteristics alone. Finally, deeper discounts need not generate larger incremental profit contributions; in the theme-park application, an intermediate discount can outperform both deeper and shallower discounts after the portfolio is re-optimized. Bundle design is a portfolio problem: a bundle's contribution depends not only on the demand it generates, but also on the customer and operational adjustments it induces elsewhere in the portfolio.

Title: Pricing and information provision in service platforms with heterogeneous customers
Authors: Xin Weng, Lijian Lu, Li Xiao
Affiliations: Fuzhou University; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; University of Macau
Abstract: Service platforms frequently employ virtual queues where customers have differing sensitivities to wait times and cannot see their precise positions in line. In these settings, providers often disclose waiting-time information to influence customers’ decisions on whether to join or balk. A natural benchmark is to report the long-term average waiting time, yet whether this deterministic disclosure policy is optimal remains unclear when both pricing and customer participation are endogenous. This study develops a stylized theoretical framework to explore the joint structure of pricing and waiting-time information disclosure for service providers managing diverse customers in a virtual queue. The provider decides on both the service price and the waiting-time disclosure policy within a rational-expectations framework. Our findings reveal that the optimal disclosure strategy is captured by scaled Rademacher distributions, meaning at most two distinct announcement values are required. This reduces a complex infinite-dimensional problem to a more manageable finite-dimensional optimization task. Leveraging this framework, we derive the optimal strategies for pricing and disclosure, identifying scenarios where variability in announced waiting times is beneficial. Our analysis shows that noise is advantageous when customers can handle uncertain wait-time signals or initially perceive the service as quick. The optimal level of noise correlates with system congestion, offering the greatest benefits when there is a notable disparity between perceived and actual congestion levels. This provides significant advantages when disclosing waiting times with noise. These findings offer actionable insights for service platforms, guiding them in creating cohesive strategies that encompass pricing, information disclosure, and service configuration, ultimately enhancing customer experience and operational efficiency.

Title: Multi-self presentation and knowledge contribution in platform operations: Evidence from a natural experiment
Authors: Yingpeng Zhu, Zike Cao, Gen Li, Yi Yang, Liangfei Qiu
Affiliations: University of Macau; Zhejiang University; Fudan University; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; University of Florida
Abstract: Operations of online user-generated content (UGC) platforms often involve tackling under-provision , wherein users lack motivation to contribute sufficient content. We study a novel design deployed to address this issue: the integration of a proprietary social feature that allows users to post casual free-form content (e.g., casual social content) alongside standard formal content on the platform. Leveraging a quasi-experiment on a large Chinese online knowledge-sharing platform, we assess the effects of integrating such a social feature on users’ formal knowledge contribution (i.e., writing answers to others’ questions ). Using difference-in-differences (DiD) analyses paired with various matching strategies, such as propensity score matching and look-ahead propensity score matching, we find that users who adopt and frequently use the feature (i.e., high adopters) show a stronger incentive to contribute answers without compromising quality. These results are further validated by a set of robustness checks. Further mediation analysis suggests that such a complementary effect might be because of two mechanisms related to the integrated social feature’s multi-self presentation function: first, the new feature increases high adopters’ engagement on the platform and leads them to consume more knowledge content, which in turn facilitates knowledge contribution; second, high adopters receive more social recognition benefits by building a more complete self through the integrated social feature, and such increased social recognition benefits further motivate more subsequent content contribution. Moreover, employing a text-mining approach to assess the semantic similarity between users’ casual social content and their formal knowledge contributions, we find that the complementary effect is amplified for high adopters whose casual posts remain more closely connected to their formal knowledge domain (i.e., are more semantically aligned with their formal knowledge). Our results have novel implications for platform design and operations to motivate users to contribute valuable content.

Title: Valuation Bottlenecks: Why Isn’t a Better Business Enough for a Higher Market Capitalization?
Authors: Shumpei Iwao, Vatsal Mitesh Tailor, Qi Wu
Abstract: Firms often improve operations, disclosure, governance, or financing capacity without an immediate and proportional market-capitalization response. Could a single unresolved concern limit the market's response to improvements elsewhere in the firm? Classical multifactor and machine-learning models ask which risks or characteristics explain or predict returns. We ask whether the relatively weakest among several coexisting firm conditions receives disproportionate valuation weight. We model equity value as the lower envelope of lens-specific valuations. A hard minimum makes one lens locally binding; a soft minimum assigns continuous, state-dependent weights. We use exploratory factor analysis on 268 accounting characteristics to construct five firm-state lenses, with membership and weights determined by the loading structure rather than by an economic taxonomy, and rank each lens within industry, size, and quarter peers. We document a weakest lens effect : beyond the additive effects of all five lens ranks, a firm's weakest lens carries an incremental association with next-quarter returns, and it survives saturated joint rank-quintile controls. Gating the test at the bottom decile and then the bottom quintile of the peer distribution, the association is concentrated among firms whose weakest lens is weak against peers and not merely lowest within the firm. In baseline soft-min specifications, it fades steadily as the gate is widened. We then investigate whether analyst attention may help explain this pattern. We use large language models on 1.7 million earnings-call questions and find that, in baseline specifications, the weakest lens attracts a larger share of questions, especially when it is also weak among peers; this cross-sectional alignment is consistent with an attention channel as one possible explanation for the observed return pattern. The framework offers managers seeking to maximize market capitalization a new perspective on prioritizing scarce managerial attention.

Title: From institutional expansion to exposure-driven co-evolution: Reinterpreting “Operations and Supply Chain Management in China”
Authors: Yinghao Pan, Dingyi Tang, Jie Wu, Yuan Sun, Liangfei Qiu
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China; University of Florida; Modern Business Research Center & School of Business Administration (MBA) & School of Management and E-Business (Cross-Border E-Commerce College), Zhejiang Gongshang University, Hangzhou, China
Abstract: This paper builds on and reinterprets “Operations and Supply Chain Management in China”, which offers a comprehensive account of the rapid institutional, educational, and research development of Operations and Supply Chain Management (OSCM) in China. While the Institutional–Dynamic–Organizational (IDO) framework effectively captures domestic structural transformation, it under-theorizes a critical external driver of this evolution: international knowledge exposure and collaboration. To address this gap, we complement the domestic institutional perspective with a bibliometric study of published articles in Production and Operations Management from 1992 to 2026. The evidence shows that China's growing presence in OSCM research is overwhelmingly collaboration-mediated, with China–U.S. co-authorship constituting the dominant channel of integration. The rise of China in top-tier OSCM journals is therefore not primarily an autonomous national trajectory, but a structurally embedded phenomenon within global co-authorship networks. Our findings suggest that China's OSCM evolution cannot be fully explained by domestic institutional expansion, policy support, or educational scaling alone. Instead, it reflects a broader process of exposure-driven co-evolution within a globally integrated knowledge system. In this system, international collaboration is not merely a byproduct of scientific development but a central mechanism shaping the structure and trajectory of global OSCM knowledge production.

Title: Mind the cost of disturbance: Firm-level supply chain risk and the bank loan cost
Authors: Daxuan Cheng, Lei Gao, Yin Liao, Zheyao Pan
Affiliations: Macquarie University; George Mason University
Abstract: This study investigates whether and how supply chain risk, a core operational vulnerability, is priced in financial credit markets. Using a novel text-based firm-level measure, we show that elevated supply chain risk leads to higher loan interest spreads. Exploiting natural disasters as exogenous shocks to production networks, we provide causal evidence that shocks increase perceived supply chain fragility and, in turn, raise borrowing costs. These effects are amplified when lenders face greater private-information deficiency, and are further strengthened when external information production is more intensive—the former heightening lenders’ concern over supply chain exposure, the latter enhancing their capacity to recognize and price it. Critically, lenders treat supply chain fragility as a form of credit risk: firms with higher supply chain risk face increased default risk, and firms whose production networks are struck by supplier disasters face a higher probability of covenant violation and tighter covenant restrictions, signaling lenders’ anticipation of repayment difficulties. Our findings highlight a new financial consequence of operational risk, showing that supply chain disruption directly affects corporate financing outcomes.

Title: The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through
Authors: Holly Dykstra, Shibeal O’ Flaherty, Ashley Whillans
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Konstanz, 78464 Konstanz, Germany; and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), 75007 Paris, France; School for Government, King’s College London, London WC2R 2LS, United Kingdom; Negotiation, Organizations & Markets Unit, Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts 02163
Abstract: Behavioral interventions often focus on reducing friction to encourage behavior change. In contrast, we provide evidence that adding initial friction to a sign-up process can increase follow-through behavior. In a field experiment with a state department of transportation ([Formula: see text]), we test whether adding modest friction during sign-up for a carpool platform increases usage. Although a more effortful sign-up process leads to 25% fewer sign-ups, overall usage increases. Importantly, these results were only partly explained by selection: Using an intent-to-treat analysis, participants with a more effortful sign-up process took 1.6 times more carpool trips per week over four months, leading to more overall trips despite fewer users. In a second experiment with online task work, participants with more effortful sign-up were 37% more likely to return the next day and completed more work overall. These results suggest that adding friction may be an overlooked strategy when follow-through, rather than initial uptake, is the primary goal. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Title: Competition and Diversity in Generative AI
Authors: Manish Raghavan
Affiliations: Sloan School of Management and Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, MIT, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139
Abstract: Recent evidence, both in the laboratory and in the wild, suggests that the use of generative artificial intelligence reduces the diversity of content produced. As generative AI penetrates more markets and reaches widespread adoption, should we still expect to see content homogenization? Our work begins with a simple observation: content producers do not act in isolation. Instead, they compete with one another (e.g., for customers or attention). We explore the impact competition has on both content diversity and overall social welfare when producers use generative AI. Through a formal game-theoretic model, we show that competitive markets select for diverse AI models, mitigating monoculture. We further show that a generative AI model that performs well in isolation (i.e., according to a benchmark) may fail to provide value in a competitive market. Our results highlight the importance of evaluating generative AI models across the breadth of their output distributions, particularly when they will be deployed in competitive environments. We validate our theoretical results with a series of experiments involving generative text and image models. Overall, our results suggest that homogenization due to generative AI is unlikely to persist under strong competition. This paper was accepted by Itai Ashlagi, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Title: Enhancing Safety Signaling: Integrating Clinical Trials and Post-Marketing Adverse Event Reports
Authors: Fernanda Bravo, Lawrence Yunliang Chen, John Silberholz
Affiliations: University of California Los Angeles, Anderson School of Management, Los Angeles, California, 90095, United States; UC Berkeley, Industrial Engineering and Operations Research Department, Berkeley, California, United States; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, OR/Stats, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 02139-4307, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) cause numerous emergency room visits and thousands of deaths annually in the U.S. Although regulators like the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) aim to detect safety issues during clinical trials, these trials are often too small, short, or restrictive to capture rare or delayed ADRs. Consequently, regulators rely on spontaneous adverse event reporting systems (eg, FAERS) to identify potential safety issues—termed safety signals—by detecting side effects that occur disproportionately among patients taking a particular drug. However, these observational data are subject to selection and reporting biases, which can lead to false signals or missed risks. Methodology/results: We propose a Bayesian framework to enhance the hypothesis generation step in safety signaling, offering two methodological advances over standard approaches that rely solely on observational data. First, it integrates pre-approval clinical trial and post-approval observational data. Second, it uses information from common ADRs to estimate and correct bias in rare ADRs. We assess the approach using an analytical model and a large-scale numerical study with real clinical trial and FAERS data. Incorporating clinical trial data substantially reduces signaling costs, and using a common ADR for debiasing yields further gains. This refinement improves decisions for about 1% of ADRs, translating to expected cost savings of 1.5–2.3% (approx. $32–159 million), with performance robust to moderate parameter misspecification. Managerial implications: By using existing regulatory data, our approach supports a more efficient and timely hypothesis generation process in post-approval surveillance.

Title: Dialysis Clinic Patient Flow and Work Design
Authors: Vincent Slaugh, Andre Augusto Cire
Affiliations: Cornell University, SC Johnson College of Business, Ithaca, New York, United States; University of Toronto Scarborough, Department of Management, Toronto, Canada
Abstract: Problem Definition: For 433,000 patients in the United States with advanced kidney failure, hemodialysis is a life-sustaining treatment. Approximately 7,600 outpatient dialysis clinics serve these patients, whose treatments cost over $25 billion annually. Each treatment involves a pre-treatment “put-on” task and a post-treatment “take-off” task performed by patient care technicians (PCTs). These frontline workers face intense, overlapping demands that can compromise patient safety and contribute to PCT burnout. We study how to jointly schedule PCTs and patients to reduce makespan and increase labor efficiency in dialysis clinic operations through better patient flow. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-ons as soon as a technician and station are free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons and the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. We derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s makespan under constant treatment durations and show that interlaced schedules achieve the shortest completion time, whereas tandem configurations can reduce labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations and stochastic task times and arrivals to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators’ attention to the primary driver of labor efficiency: minimizing the time that stations sit unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies of the push approach for a single pod, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system while increasing the standard time allotted for tasks can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-on tasks for treatment as soon as a station is free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons, the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. Under standard conditions, we derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s completion time and show that interlacing finishes earliest with homogeneous treatment durations, while tandem configurations can lower labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators’ attention to what is most important for labor efficiency: minimizing the time that a station is unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies associated with the push approach, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system with increased standard task times can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks.

Title: Response efficiency versus response customization: An examination of firms’ responses to platform-empowered group complaints
Authors: Zilong Liu, Xuequn Wang, Xin (Robert) Luo, Chaoqun Chu, Tingting Song
Affiliations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics; University of New Mexico; Hong Kong Metropolitan University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: The rise of group complaints on digital platforms, where consumers can publicly voice collective concerns, presents significant challenges for firms’ service recovery operations. Prior research assessing service operations on digital platforms has focused primarily on individual complaints, and less is known about how firms respond to platform-empowered (PE) group complaints. We examine this question through the lens of a trade-off between response efficiency and response customization and argue that this trade-off evolves as group complaints develop over time. Based on a large-scale dataset from Tousu, a leading complaint platform in China, we find that group complaints paradoxically increase response time and decrease empathy and explanation in firms’ responses. Further analyses indicate that these effects depend on dynamic group size and dynamic need diversity. When dynamic need diversity is low, larger groups are associated with more standardized, efficiency-oriented responses, whereas when dynamic need diversity is high, larger groups are associated with slower but more customized responses. These findings extend research on service operations by showing how PE group complaints reshape firms’ complaint handling. Our study also provides operational guidance for managing group complaints more effectively.

Title: Retail on Wheels: A Time-Sensitive Traveling Salesman Problem
Authors: Zhuolun Dong, Junyu Cao, Wei Qi
Affiliations: McCombs School of Business, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712; Department of Industrial Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China
Abstract: Rapid advancement in self-driving technology has brought mobile retail into the spotlight. Motivated by its potential, we present a model, theory, and insights into the operations of mobile retail, where a fleet of wheeled stores traverses a service region, selectively seeks locations in which to perch, and fulfills local customer demand. The goal of retailers is to strike a balance between perching and migrating to maximize total revenue. To dispatch such stores, retailers need to consider the following time-sensitive factors: (i) how busy the service is, (ii) how soon customers will arrive, and (iii) how quickly freshness decays. We propose and analyze a model that incorporates these factors into the classical traveling salesman problem (TSP), which we call the “time-sensitive TSP.” Using the continuous approximation approach, we derive the optimal revenue as well as the upper and lower bounds in the asymptotic regime as candidate locations increase to infinity. The tightness of the bounds is validated. Our analysis demonstrates that store mobility creates value by bringing proximity to customers. We further uncover the effects of these time-sensitive features on decision making. Specifically, the scaling relationship between revenue and fleet size is affected by customer tardiness and busyness. Busyness determines stores’ ability to expand their service, whereas tardiness affects how effectively stores can utilize the initial high-freshness period. These findings deepen our understanding of mobile retail operations. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: J. Cao acknowledges the support from McCombs Research Excellence Grant. W. Qi acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72242106, 72188101, and 72521001].
