Title: Shipment Monitoring, Allocation, and the Impact on Food Waste
Authors: Tao Lu
Affiliations: School of Business, University of Connecticut, Storrs, Connecticut 06269
Abstract: Often advocated for the potential to reduce waste in fresh produce supply chains, sensor technologies enable firms to monitor the condition of each product unit and allocate them to markets at different transportation distances, thereby matching units with shorter shelf lives with closer markets. In this paper, we consider a firm purchasing and transporting a fresh produce product for sale in two destination markets. Postharvest processes cause a proportion of the product to be in risky condition, potentially becoming unsalable (“spoiled”) due to shelf-life deterioration during transportation. With monitoring technology, the firm first determines a purchase quantity and then decides how to allocate each unit (in either good or risky condition) between markets. We characterize the optimal allocation policies, which can be used to efficiently determine the optimal purchase quantity. Our analysis shows that such technology may inadvertently increase total waste by inducing larger purchase quantities; this increase is often, but not always, accompanied by a lower waste rate and improved distribution efficiency. As firms increasingly adopt monitoring technology for shipment allocation, additional policy and managerial attention may be required. Improvements in postharvest processes can strengthen the waste-reduction benefits of monitoring technology. Firms seeking to maintain their sustainability goals can capture most of the profit gains from monitoring by carefully moderating increases in purchase quantities. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07382 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management.

Title: A Continuous-Time Model of Subscription and Repeat Purchase
Authors: Wee Chaimanowong, Tony Ke
Affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Marketing, Shatin, Hong Kong
Abstract: Problem definition: We present a continuous-time model of consumers’ joint decisions of membership subscription and repeat purchase. A consumer pays a flow membership fee; her valuation follows a Brownian motion, purchase needs arrive via a Poisson process, and she chooses whether to buy and when to unsubscribe. The model is analytically tractable thanks to the connection between consumer lifetime and hitting time of Brownian motions. Methodology/results: Consumers’ unsubscription decision solves an optimal-stopping problem with a closed-form valuation cutoff; purchase occurs when valuation exceeds the transaction price. These thresholds generate three fluid consumer modes—buyer, tracker, and churner. We find that consumers who are about to terminate subscription tend to purchase less frequently, and who are currently subscribing are more likely to continue subscription. This endogenous customer loyalty is captured by a one-parameter retention formula [Formula: see text], which can accommodate rapid early attrition and an asymptotic slow decay. Managerial implications: For empirical estimation, we cast latent-valuation filtering as a heat-diffusion problem and develop a kernel-iteration likelihood approximation with vanishing discretization errors. Three empirical studies that feature two distinct firm-customer relationships demonstrate that our model performs on par with or better than existing models. Based on the model estimates, firms can infer consumers’ latent engagement and churn risk from purchase histories and devise the optimal package of membership fee and transaction price.

Title: Operations Management in the Sharing Economy: Advances, Challenges, and Opportunities
Authors: Huan Cao, Liu Ming, Daehoon Noh, David Simchi-Levi, Tunay Tunca, Yi Xu, Weiming Zhu
Affiliations: Lyft Inc, Marketplace, San Francisco, California, United States; Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzen, Business School, China; Korea University, Logistics, Service, and Operations Management, Seongbuk-gu, Seoul, Korea (the Republic of); Massachusetts Institute of Technology, OR Center, LIDS and IDSS, Massachusetts, United States; University of Maryland, DOIT, College Park, Maryland, United States; University of Maryland, DOIT, United States; Universidad de Navarra IESE Business School, Production, Technology and Operations Management, Barcelona, Catalunya, Spain
Abstract: The rapid growth of the sharing economy over the past decade has changed many industries in profound ways. The innovative business models that have emerged in the sharing economy present unique opportunities as well as challenges, which have attracted a significant amount of attention from researchers in the operations management field. In this paper, we discuss the advances, challenges, and opportunities for research on operations management in the sharing economy. We divide sharing economy into eight categories: Ride Sharing, Space Sharing, Bike Sharing, Vehicle Sharing, Group Buying, Crowdfunding, Freelancing, and Last-Mile Delivery. For each business category, we identify the gaps and current challenges in the existing literature, discuss emerging industry trends and research topics, and suggest several future research directions. Our goal is to stimulate discussion and ideas about future studies in this area.

Title: Online Decisions with (Biased) Offline Data
Authors: Hyun-Soo Ahn, Mengzhenyu Zhang, Zijin Zhang
Affiliations: Stephen M. Ross School of Business, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109; School of Management, University College London, London E14 5AA, United Kingdom; Carroll School of Management, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts 02467
Abstract: Making Better Decisions with Imperfect Historical Data Historical data can provide valuable information for online decision making, but its usefulness may be limited when the environment has changed. In “Online Decisions with (Biased) Offline Data,” Ahn, Zhang, and Zhang study how firms can combine potentially biased offline data with newly collected online observations in two canonical operations management problems: dynamic inventory decisions and dynamic pricing. The authors develop two online learning policies that balance the benefits of historical information against the risk of relying on data from a different distribution. The soft-switch policy automatically adjusts the reliance on offline and online data without requiring prior knowledge of the degree of bias. The hard-switch policy instead uses information about the magnitude of the distributional shift to determine when to rely primarily on online data. Both policies achieve optimal regret up to a logarithmic factor, whereas the analysis quantifies how the value of offline data depends on its size and bias.

Title: Operations management for sustainable development and public policy making
Authors: Jan C Fransoo, Guan-Yuan Wang, Simone Balvers
Affiliations: Tilburg University
Abstract: Public policy making often faces challenges in implementation due to a lack of attention to operational realities. Operations management (OM) research, with its strong empirical component and focus on detailed model-based mechanisms, offers unique insights for successful policy execution. This paper explores the synergies between economics, development economics, and OM in addressing public policy implementation, arguing that OM’s process-level understanding, empirical rigor, and focus on operational feasibility can enhance policy design and evaluation. We illustrate this potential through examples from sustainability and social development, demonstrating how OM can bridge the gap between economic policy insights and operational execution.

Title: Music Marketing with Generative AI
Authors: Benedikt Roder, Jochen Hartmann
Affiliations: Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany; Technical University of Munich, Munchen, Germany
Abstract: The multibillion-dollar music industry faces severe content creation bottlenecks, making multimedia marketing assets prohibitively costly for smaller artists. This practice paper introduces a Marketing Asset Generation Engine (MAGE) that can produce over 700 million video ad variations reflecting each artist’s visual identity using only a music track’s audio and album cover as inputs. Collaborating with one of the world’s largest music labels, we conduct four preregistered field studies with over 11 million impressions across 75 campaigns for 33 music tracks on TikTok and Meta to validate MAGE. First, pooled across studies, MAGE-generated ads significantly outperform human-designed ads on TikTok with on average 26% higher click-through rates and 10% higher engagement, while we do not detect statistically significant performance differences on Meta, all at 98% lower production cost. Second, neither marketing professionals nor laypeople can reliably identify winning ads such that random sampling of MAGE’s outputs performs as well as human-curated selections. In contrast, an AI-in-the-loop system trained on past performance data can predict pre-launch which MAGE-generated ads will perform best for specific audience segments. These findings demonstrate that generative AI democratizes music marketing by making effective, on-brand video ads accessible at scale.

Title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
Authors: Erdem Dogukan Yilmaz, Ivana Naumovska, Vikas A. Aggarwal
Affiliations: INSEAD, 77305 Fontainebleau, France
Abstract: We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .

Title: Why Do We Discriminate? Directional Beliefs and Biased Information Processing
Authors: Markus Eyting
Affiliations: Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, 55128 Mainz, Germany; and Leibniz Institute for Financial Research Sustainable Architecture for Finance in Europe, 60323 Frankfurt am Main, Germany
Abstract: Identifying the cause of discrimination is crucial to designing effective policies and to understanding discrimination dynamics. This paper provides a potential link between existing models of taste-based and statistical discrimination by studying directional belief formation through biased information search and processing. By selectively acquiring and processing information, individuals form directional beliefs and consequently discriminate based on these beliefs. Through a series of experiments in which individuals endogenously acquire and process various signals, I document discrimination stemming from directional beliefs and demonstrate important differences in how it manifests compared with taste-based and statistical discrimination. Finally, I show that limiting individuals’ scope to interpret information reduces such discrimination. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Title: Systemically Important Banks and Loan Performance: Evidence from India
Authors: Shashwat Agrawal, Nishant Kashyap, Sriniwas Mahapatro, Prasanna Tantri
Affiliations: Department of Finance, Carroll School of Management, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, Boston, Massachusetts 02467; Finance and Accounting Area, Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad, Vastrapur, Ahmedabad, Gujarat 380015, India; Department of Finance and Accounting, Saunders College of Business, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, New York 14623; Finance Area, Indian School of Business, Gachibowli, Hyderabad, Telangana 500032, India
Abstract: We examine whether designating banks as systemically important affects loan performance in an emerging-market setting where such banks are large domestic institutions and market imperfections make monitoring crucial for loan performance. Using loan-level data and the staggered designation of banks as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (DSIBs) in India, we find that loan performance deteriorates following DSIB designation. The evidence points to bank-level moral hazard as the underlying mechanism: DSIBs reduce postorigination monitoring and weaken loan recovery efforts. Borrowers respond accordingly, exhibiting poorer financial health and loan repayment, particularly on loans extended by DSIBs. This paper was accepted by Jan Bouwens, accounting. Title: Competition for Customer Attention is Creating Oversupply Pockets in US Micromobility
Authors: Hale Erkan, Ashish Agarwal, Kumar Muthuraman, Ioannis Stamatopoulos
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, IROM, Austin, Texas, 78705, United States; The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, IROM, Austin, Texas, United States; University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, Information, Risk, and Operations Management, Austin, Texas, 78705, United States
Abstract: We present analytical and empirical arguments that competition over a nearly homogeneous service forces operators to oversupply scooters in urban centers. First, using deployment and ride data from operator APIs and city transportation departments, as well as telemetry data from one of the top three U.S. operators, we estimate average daily scooter utilization across nine major U.S. cities at 3.9%—half the 7.7% minimum utilization target set by transportation departments. Second, using a parsimonious game-theoretic model, we argue that if riders choose among available scooters roughly at random (e.g., the closest one), then in equilibrium all operators need to inflate their fleet sizes to preserve their market shares. Third, using granular data on riders’ choice sets and choices from Kansas City, MO, we provide evidence that these choices are indeed roughly random. Fourth, using our structurally estimated game-theoretic model, we find that in Kansas City, MO: (i) there is a 406% oversupply of scooters, (ii) the interaction between rider choice and competition accounts for 81% of this oversupply, and (iii) if the transportation department issued one more operator permit, oversupply would increase by an additional 82 pp. We conclude that transportation departments should be frugal with the number of permits they issue, and should welcome the consolidation of the scooter market.

Title: Learning Optimal Classification Trees Robust to Distribution Shifts
Authors: Nathan Lawrence Justin, Sina Aghaei, Andres Gomez, Phebe Vayanos
Affiliations: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, 90089-0001, United States; University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, United States; University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, 90089, United States; University of Southern California Viterbi School of Engineering, Industrial & Systems Engineering, Los Angeles, California, 90089, United States
Abstract: We consider the problem of learning classification trees that are robust to distribution shifts between training and testing/deployment data. This problem arises frequently in high stakes settings such as public health and social work where data is often collected using self-reported surveys which are highly sensitive to e.g., the framing of the questions, the time when and place where the survey is conducted, and the level of comfort the interviewee has in sharing information with the interviewer. We propose a method for learning optimal robust classification trees based on mixed-integer robust optimization technology. In particular, we demonstrate that the problem of learning an optimal robust tree can be cast as a single-stage mixed-integer robust optimization problem with a highly nonlinear and discontinuous objective. We reformulate this problem equivalently as a two-stage linear robust optimization problem for which we devise a tailored solution procedure based on constraint generation. We evaluate the performance of our approach on numerous publicly available datasets, and compare the performance to a regularized, non-robust optimal tree. We show an increase of up to 12.48 percentage points in worst-case accuracy and of up to 4.85 percentage points in average-case accuracy across several datasets and distribution shifts from using our robust solution in comparison to the non-robust one.

Title: Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming for Log-linear Autoregressive Uncertainty in the Right-hand Side
Authors: Christian Füllner, Steffen Rebennack
Affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Germany; Karlsruher Institute of Technology (KIT), Institute of Operations Research, Karlsruhe, Germany
Abstract: We consider the generation of cuts in stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) for multistage stochastic linear programming problems with stagewise dependent uncertainty in the right-hand side described by a nonlinear autoregressive process. We first derive cut formulas for the general nonlinear autoregressive process. For these general cuts, the computational tractability becomes a major challenge for SDDP-type algorithms. We are, however, able to develop tractable closed-form cut formulas for the special case of log-linear autoregressive processes. The obtained cuts are in general non-convex in the history of the stochastic process, but still linear in all decision variables, and thus can be directly incorporated into the subproblems in SDDP without compromising their linearity. If solvers do not allow for this, our formulas can be used to adapt the intercept of a given cut to a scenario at hand in a computationally tractable way. In this sense, cuts generated for one specific scenario are shared with other scenarios. Our findings are supported by a computational study of a hydrothermal scheduling problem, which demonstrates a favorable performance of our proposed version of SDDP compared to approaches from the literature.

Title: Comment Letters, Connected Investors, and Corporate Bond Issuance
Authors: Yi Ding, T. J. Wong, Ray Zhang, Tianyu Zhang
Affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Shenzhen 518172, China; University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90089; Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, British Columbia V5A 1S6, Canada
Abstract: Using a proprietary data set that documents corporate bond issuances in China, we find that bond regulators’ comment letters (CLs) on issuers’ public disclosures generally target opaque firms and reduce bond issuance success. We also find, however, that connected investors—financial institutions with prior business relationships with the issuers—purchase a relatively larger share of bond issuances from CL recipients than from non-CL recipients, and this greater participation contributes to overpricing. Further analysis shows that connected investors support CL recipients because they possess superior private information and obtain private benefits from their connections. Title: Optimality of Public Persuasion for Single-Good Allocation
Authors: Chen Chen, Xuyuanda Qi
Affiliations: New York University Shanghai, Shanghai 200124, China
Abstract: When Sharing the Same Information Is Optimal Should a school advisor tailor recommendation letters to different employers or share the same information with everyone? Similar questions arise in start-up fundraising and biotech partnerships. In “Optimality of Public Persuasion for Single-Good Allocation,” Chen and Qi study how a sender can strategically disclose information when allocating an indivisible good to at most one self-interested receiver. The sender may send tailored private messages to individual receivers or publicly broadcast the same information to everyone. Surprisingly, the authors show that, when the sender has a known preference ordering over receivers, public persuasion is optimal even if receivers can subsequently communicate and share information. The optimal public mechanism can be derived from a simpler first-best allocation problem subject only to receivers’ participation constraints. The authors also develop a dual approach to characterize the structure of optimal mechanisms when the good’s characteristics are captured by a one-dimensional variable and all receivers’ utility functions are linear in this variable and reveal an intriguing decoupling structure.

Title: Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange
Authors: Weixiao Huang, Carlos Morel Figueroa, Arjun Venat, Sarah E. Stanlick, Yunus D. Telliel, Alexander Teytelboym, Jennifer A. Pazour, Andrew C. Trapp
Affiliations: Business School, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, New York 12180; Department of Computer Science, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Integrative and Global Studies, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Humanities & Arts, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Economics, University of Oxford, Oxford OX1 3UQ, United Kingdom; and Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, New York 12180
Abstract: Unlocking Value Through Nonprofit Resource Sharing Nonprofit organizations often operate under tight budgets while idle equipment, unused space, and shareable skills and expertise are frequently underutilized, with existing resource exchanges in the nonprofit sector limited to bilateral barter or relatively homogeneous resources. In “Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange,” Huang et al. propose Sharing With a Purpose (SWAP), a resource-sharing system that enables nonprofits to exchange heterogeneous resources without monetary payments. SWAP combines an auction-based process, SWAPcredit valuation, and integer optimization to facilitate multilateral exchanges, allowing nonprofits to obtain needed resources by contributing resources of their own. The authors implement this market design through the SWAP Hub, a digital platform deployed with nonprofit communities in multiple regions. Through repeated exchange episodes, participating organizations have shared not only physical assets but also a wide range of skills, services, and expertise, including marketing, management, event planning, and organizational development. The study demonstrates how innovative market design can unlock latent value in community resources, alleviate resource constraints, and encourage new connections and collaboration among nonprofit organizations.

Title: Nutrient legacies from elephant megacarcasses create coldspots of biodiversity and hotspots of ecosystem processes
Authors: Courtney G. Reed, Nathan P. Lemoine, Michelle L. Budny, Vincent C. Clarke, Johan T. du Toit, Ryan Helcoski, Helga Knoetze, Jane M. Lucas, Joshua P. Schimel, Izak P. J. Smit, Tercia Strydom, Aimee G. Tallian, Dave I. Thompson, Deron E. Burkepile
Affiliations: Marine Science Institute, University of California; Department of Biological Sciences, Marquette University; Department of Zoology, Milwaukee Public Museum; Unit for Environmental Sciences and Management, North West University; Department of Wildland Resources and the Ecology Center, Utah State University; Institute of Zoology, Zoological Society of London; The Expanded Freshwater and Terrestrial Environmental Observation Network; Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies; Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Marine Biology, University of California; Scientific Services, South African National Parks; Sustainability Research Unit & CNRS-NMU International Research Laboratory, REHABS, Nelson Mandela University; Department of Zoology and Entomology, University of Pretoria; Scientific Services South African National Parks; Soil, Crop, and Climate Sciences, University of the Free State; Division of Land and Biodiversity, Norwegian Institute for Nature Research; South African Environmental Observation Network, Ndlovu Node, WITS Rural Campus; School of Animal, Plant and Environmental Sciences, University of the Witwatersrand
Abstract: Terrestrial megafauna (animals >1,000 kg) have substantial impacts on ecosystems while alive; yet, we know little about the impacts of these ecosystem engineers after they die. Like whale carcasses in the ocean, terrestrial megacarcasses may leave ecological legacies via the nutrient pulses they create on the landscape. Here, we investigated the impact of elephant megacarcasses on savanna ecosystems in Kruger National Park, South Africa. To determine how elephant carcasses affect below- and aboveground biodiversity and ecosystem processes, we collected soil and plant samples from 40 carcass sites (pairing “on carcass” and “off carcass” samples) ranging from 8 d to 7.7 y postmortem. We found that elephant carcasses released enormous pools of nutrients into savanna soils, increasing ammonium by 31×, nitrate by 7×, and phosphorus by 3× on average. These extreme ammonium concentrations were negatively correlated with the biodiversity of bacteria and plants, which were both suppressed at elephant carcass sites. Despite these decreases in biodiversity, ecosystem processes were strongly elevated at elephant carcass sites, with soil microbial respiration elevated for 1 to 2 y and herbivore grazing >3× higher for 7+ y postmortem. These results demonstrate that elephant megacarcasses generate coldspots of biodiversity but hotspots of ecosystem processes, unveiling a cryptic ecological function of megaherbivores that is extreme in both magnitude and duration relative to carcasses of smaller animals. As humans drive terrestrial megafauna toward extinction, we risk losing not only their ecosystem engineering abilities while they are alive but also the ecological legacies their carcasses create after death.

Title: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South
Authors: Mingxing Chen, Wenming Song, Dadao Lu, Yu Deng, Chenglong Wang, Huiping Jiang, Yuyu Zhou, Murray W. Scown, Liangkan Chen, Jing Ma, Heran Zheng, Xuemei Bai
Affiliations: Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences; Key Laboratory of Regional Sustainable Development Modeling, Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences; College of Resource and Environment, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences; School of Geography and Ocean Science, Nanjing University; Department of Geography and Institute for Climate and Carbon Neutrality, The University of Hong Kong; Lund University Centre for Sustainability Studies, Lund University; The Bartlett School of Sustainable Construction, University College London; Fenner School of Environment and Society, Australian National University; Institute for Future Initiatives, The University of Tokyo, 7-3-1 Hongo
Abstract: Informal settlements are widespread and rapidly growing, often associated with high vulnerabilities. However, global-scale understanding on their spatial distribution and complexity of vulnerability is limited. Here, we delineate the informal settlements across a sample of 1,914 cities of the Global South by integrating Sentinel-2 imagery with deep learning models, and we explore the heterogeneity of vulnerability using Urban Informal Settlement Vulnerability Index that encompasses living conditions, social infrastructure, and environmental risk. We found that Urban Informal Settlements cover 12.94 ± 2.52% of their total urban areas (approximately 34.04 × 10 3 km 2 ), especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Middle Asia. Sub-Saharan African cities have the highest vulnerability of informal settlements, with 31.75 ± 6.20% of total urban areas being occupied by informal settlements, while East Asian cities exhibit relatively low vulnerability across all dimensions. We also find that urban informal settlements with high environmental exposure are widespread in the Global South, and there is a significantly polarized distribution between “low” and “high” vulnerability categories. The findings highlight the disparate distribution of multidimensional vulnerability in informal settlements across the Urban South, providing a comparative evidence base for further local assessment and context-specific policy discussions related to SDG 11.

Title: Field experiments predict ecological response to a large-scale epidemic of an anti-keystone pathogen
Authors: J. Timothy Wootton, Khashiff Miranda, Amy K. Henry, Catherine A. Pfister
Affiliations: Department of Ecology and Evolution, University of Chicago; Committee on Evolutionary Biology, University of Chicago; Department of Biology, Université Laval; Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of California
Abstract: Knowledge of how pathogens, in the context of a changing environment, shape the structure of ecological communities remains limited, and little information exists on the ability of small-scale field experiments to predict the consequences of large-scale environmental impacts. We addressed these issues using the emergence of a widespread epidemic (sea star wasting disease, SSWD) on rocky intertidal shorelines. Prior experiments demonstrated strong reductions in sessile species diversity in response to the local experimental removal of the sea star Pisaster ochraceus [R. T. Paine, Am. Nat. 100 , 65–75 (1966); R. T. Paine, Oceologia 15 , 93–120 (1974)] at our site. In surveys of sea star populations over 8 y spanning the onset of the SSWD epidemic, P. ochraceus populations declined by 90%, then subsequently recovered to about one third of pre-epidemic size under an endemic disease phase. Using four different types of temporal data, we documented large increases in populations of the competitively dominant mussel Mytilus californianus following P. ochraceus decline, which were of similar magnitude to those observed in prior field experiments. As in the field experiments, sessile species richness and diversity declined strongly following the onset of the SSWD epidemic as mussels were released from predator control. Our results reveal a strong effect of a pathogen in regulating ecological community structure by disrupting the role of a keystone species, a result anticipated by prior small-scale field experiments.

Title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
Authors: Nicolò Pagan, Petter Törnberg, Christopher A. Bail, Christopher Barrie
Affiliations: Department of Informatics, University of Zurich; Institute for Logic, Language and Computation, University of Amsterdam; Department of Sociology, Computer Science, Political Science, and Public Policy, Duke University; Department of Sociology, New York University; Department of Sociology, University of Oxford
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

Title: Laundering and evasion in response to antislavery policies in Brazil’s cattle sector
Authors: Tara Mittelberg, Marin E. Skidmore, Juliana L. S. C. Brandão, Lisa L. Rausch, Holly K. Gibbs
Affiliations: Nelson Institute for Environmental Studies, Center for Sustainability and the Global Environment, University of Wisconsin–Madison; Department of Agricultural and Applied Economics, University of Wisconsin–Madison; Department of Agricultural and Consumer Economics, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
Abstract: Modern slavery remains pervasive across many economic sectors. Progress toward eradicating it has been partially hindered by a lack of tested, comprehensive policy responses. Using data on millions of cattle transactions in Brazil, we evaluated how ranchers changed their selling behavior after being added to the “Dirty List,” a public registry that names and shames employers found to use modern slavery. Dirty Listed ranchers significantly reduced direct sales to slaughterhouses that signed sustainable supply chain commitments but evaded sanctions by laundering cattle through compliant intermediaries or selling to nonsignatory slaughterhouses. These responses weakened the financial cost of listing to ranchers, and likely allowed beef and leather linked to modern slave labor to enter international supply chains. Our findings highlight the limits of downstream enforcement and underscore the need to monitor upstream suppliers to ensure slavery-free supply chains.

Title: Evolution shapes ecosystem resilience through spatial self-organization
Authors: Xiaoli Dong, Alexander J. Richardson, Rachata Muneepeerakul
Affiliations: Department of Environmental Science and Policy, University of California; Department of Mathematics, University of California; Department of Agricultural and Biological Engineering, University of Florida
Abstract: Drylands are globally widespread and ecologically important but vulnerable to climate change. Many exhibit spatially self-organized vegetation patterns that enhance resilience by enabling vegetation to reorganize their patterns under drying, thereby optimizing water use and maintaining productivity. Plants can also undergo evolution in response to environmental change. Although both spatial self-organization and rapid evolution are fundamental mechanisms of resilience, their interaction remains largely unknown. Using a theoretical model, we examine how these mechanisms interact to shape vegetation transitions—abrupt or gradual—and ecosystem resilience under climatic drying. We find that pattern formation can suppress adaptation by maintaining soil moisture beneath vegetation patches despite rainfall decline, thereby limiting selection for increased drought tolerance. However, this suppression is largely alleviated under the variable rainfall typical of drylands. In turn, evolution feeds back on self-organization by increasing the spatial plasticity of vegetation patterns and their ability to reorganize under changing climate, although this positive effect weakens as evolutionary rate increases. Considering direct (adaptation) and indirect (pattern-mediated) effects, evolution enhances resilience, with indirect effects via pattern plasticity dominating. Within model scenarios spanning plausible rainfall variability and relative evolutionary-to-ecological rates, more than half of vegetation transitions are abrupt involving biomass losses exceeding 50%, highlighting a potential mechanism underlying recent global observations of widespread abrupt vegetation losses in drylands. These results demonstrate that evolution and spatial self-organization jointly determine dryland resilience under environmental change and highlight the unexpected role of evolution in patterned landscapes, calling for integrative approaches to predict ecosystem responses in a changing world.

Title: Integrating cooperative breeding with reciprocity and culture extends Hamilton’s rule to humans
Authors: Alessandra Cassar, Daniel Friedman, Shreeja Guha, Timothy Wilkins
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of San Francisco; Department of Economics, University of Essex; Department of Economics, University of California
Abstract: We study how kinship and reciprocity shape giving and child care support in societies with limited access to markets. Extending Hamilton’s rule to incorporate reciprocity, we test it using behavioral data from dictator games and surveys in remote matrilocal and patrilocal villages of northeast India (N = 406 parents of young children). We replicate with data from urban Manila neighborhoods (N = 301) and the Solomon Islands (N = 624). Consistent with predictions, transfers to recipients increase with genetic relatedness to the donor and even more with relatedness to the donor’s child—a hallmark of reciprocity anchored in shared genetic investment. Nonanonymous conditions amplify giving, especially to nonkin. Cultural norms shape cooperation, but do not trump genetic relatedness. These results underscore the role of affinal ties and reciprocal exchange in sustaining cooperation, and suggest a mechanism through which cooperative breeding could contribute to the emergence of generalized reciprocity and human sociality.

Title: The Effect of Small Quasi-Cash Rewards on Prosocial Behavior: The Case of Voluntary Plasma Donations
Authors: Stijn Bruers, Erwin Ooghe, Erik Schokkaert
Affiliations: Department of Economics, KU Leuven, 3000 Leuven, Belgium; and CESifo, 81679 Munich, Germany
Abstract: To better understand how prosocial behavior can be effectively encouraged, we study four unresolved issues: whether small rewards also motivate prosocial behavior, how short-term effects differ from longer-run behavioral adjustments, whether incentives induce substitution away from other prosocial activities, and whether reminders about existing rewards meaningfully influence behavior. We examine these issues in a long-run randomized field experiment across 12 donation centers of the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders. Donors normally receive one thank-you-coupon (worth €1.5) for a blood donation and two coupons for a plasma donation. Informing donors about the existing rewards increases plasma donations by 4.6% during the nine-month information period, although this effect fades with repeated reminders. Rewarding plasma donors with an extra coupon raises plasma donations by an additional 7.1% during the six-month reward period; this effect grows during the reward period but disappears immediately afterward. We also document a substitution effect; the plasma reward reduces blood donations by 3.3%. Survey evidence suggests that small rewards act as signals of increased need or as gifts eliciting reciprocity and that our findings may extend to volunteering decisions more broadly. Title: Modeling collective action in POM: The Strategy–Operations–People framework
Authors: Guillaume Roels, Ludo Van der Heyden
Affiliations: INSEAD
Abstract: While many business situations relevant to production and operations management (POM), such as supply chain coordination or sustainable operations, involve some form of collective action; managerial frameworks for collective action rarely appear in POM contexts. Valuable insights may thus be missed, reducing the effectiveness and implementability of the proposed POM solutions. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a framework for collective action that has its roots in the organizational behavior literature. We formalize it mathematically not only to offer definitional clarity, but also to relate it to common POM modeling approaches. We then illustrate its relevance to POM by mapping it to case studies in supply chain coordination and sustainable operations. The proposed framework, named the Strategy–Operations–People (SOP) framework, is structured in three levels, comprising three elements, two elements, and one element, respectively. First, the Strategy level induces and enforces solidarity among all team members by specifying common goals, shared values, and well-defined rules. Second, the Operations level organizes the decentralized execution of collective action in autonomous subgroups through a detailed specification of roles and processes. Third, the People level requires the individual commitment of all team members to the proposed collective action program, since a team’s performance rests on the individual contributions of its members. The framework thus addresses the common, subgroup, and individual dimensions of collective action. The SOP framework also contributes to the broader fields of team leadership and organizational behavior in two ways. First, its mathematical formalization brings operational clarity on the defining scope of the framework’s elements. Second, mapping the framework to two problems in supply chain management and sustainable operations illustrates its broad applicability, moving beyond collective action within organizations, to guide collective action taking place across organizations.

Authors: Gayatri Mishra
